text:
This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

The artist-led backlash against AI is well underway. While plenty of people are still enjoying letting their imaginations run wild with popular text-to-image models like DALL-E 2, Midjourney, and Stable Diffusion, artists are increasingly fed up with the new status quo. 

Some have united in protest against the tech sector’s common practice of indiscriminately scraping their visual work off the internet  to train their models. Artists have staged protests on popular art platforms such as DeviantArt and Art Station, or left the platforms entirely. Some have even filed lawsuits over copyright.  

Right now, there is total power asymmetry between rich and influential technology companies and artists, says Ben Zhao, a computer science professor at the University of Chicago. “The training companies can do whatever the heck they want,” Zhao says. 

But a new tool developed by Zhao’s lab might change that power dynamic. It’s called Nightshade, and it works by making subtle changes to the pixels of the image—changes that are invisible to the human eye but trick machine-learning models into thinking the image depicts something different from what it actually does. When artists apply it to their work and those images are then hoovered up as training data, these “poisoned pixels” make their way into the AI model’s data set, and cause the model to malfunction. Images of dogs become cats, hats become toasters, cars become cows. The results are really impressive, and there is currently no known defense. Read more from my story here. 

Some companies, such as OpenAI and Stability AI, have offered to let artists opt out of training sets, or have said they will respect requests not to have their work scraped. However, there’s no mechanism to force companies to stay true to their word right now. Zhao says Nightshade could be that mechanism. It is extremely expensive to build and train generative AI models, and it could be very risky for tech companies to scrape data that could break their crown jewels. 

Autumn Beverly, an artist who intends to use Nightshade, says she found her work had been scraped into the populace LAION-5B data set, and that felt very “violating.” 

“I never would have agreed to that, and [AI companies] just took it without any consent or notification or anything,” she says.

Before tools like Nightshade, Beverly did not feel comfortable sharing her work online. Beverly and other artists are calling for tech companies to shift from opt-out mechanisms to asking for consent first, and to start compensating artists for their contributions. These demands would involve some truly revolutionary changes to how the AI sector usually functions, yet she remains hopeful. 

“I’m hoping that it makes it where things have to be through consent—otherwise, they’re going to just have a broken system,” Beverly says. “That is the entire goal for me.” 

But artists are the canary in the coal mine. Their fight belongs to anyone who has ever posted anything they care about online. Our personal data, social media posts, song lyrics, news articles, fiction, even our faces—anything that is freely available online could end up in an AI model forever without our knowing about it. 

Tools like Nightshade could be a first step in tipping the power balance back to us. 

Deeper Learning

How Meta and AI companies recruited striking actors to train AI

Earlier this year, a company called Realeyes ran an “emotion study.” It recruited actors and then captured audio and video data of their voices, faces, and movements, which it fed into an AI database. That database is being used to help train virtual avatars for Meta. The project coincided with Hollywood’s historic strikes. With the industry at a standstill, the larger-than-usual number of out-of-work actors may have been a boon for Meta and Realeyes: here was a new pool of “trainers”—and data points—perfectly suited to teaching their AI to appear more human. 

Who owns your face: Many actors across the industry worry that AI—much like the models described in the emotion study—could be used to replace them, whether or not their exact faces are copied. Read more from Eileen Guo here.

Bits and Bytes

How China plans to judge generative AI safety
The Chinese government has a new draft document that proposes detailed rules for how to determine whether a generative AI model is problematic. Our China tech writer Zeyi Yang unpacks it for us. (MIT Technology Review) 

AI chatbots can guess your personal information from what you type
New research has found that large language models are excellent at guessing people’s private information from chats. This could be used to supercharge profiling for advertisements, for example. (Wired) 

OpenAI claims its new tool can detect images by DALL-E with 99% accuracy
OpenAI executives say the company is developing the tool after leading AI companies made a voluntary pledge to the White House to develop watermarks and other detection mechanisms for AI-generated content. Google announced its watermarking tool in August. (Bloomberg)

AI models fail miserably in transparency
When Stanford University tested how transparent large language models are, it found that the top-scoring model, Meta’s LLaMA 2, only scored 54 out of 100. Growing opacity is a worrying trend in AI. AI models are going to have huge societal influence, and we need more visibility into them to be able to hold them accountable. (Stanford) 

A college student built an AI system to read 2,000-year-old Roman scrolls
How fun! A 21-year-old computer science major developed an AI program to decipher ancient Roman scrolls that were damaged by a volcanic eruption in the year 79. The program was able to detect about a dozen letters, which experts translated into the word “porphyras”—ancient Greek for purple.  (The Washington Post)

text:
🌍 WORLD NEWS REPORT
November 13, 2026 | A World at a Crossroads
War, Political Change, Economic Pressure, Climate Challenges and Humanity's Future
🇺🇸 1. UNITED STATES: DEMOCRATS RESHAPE CONGRESS
America's November 3 midterm elections produced a sweeping Democratic victory. Democrats secured both the House of Representatives and Senate, dramatically changing the political landscape confronting President Donald Trump.

Voters expressed frustration over living costs, inflation and government policies. Democrats gained more than 40 Republican-held House seats. The new Congress, beginning in January 2027, will have stronger oversight authority, although presidential veto powers remain.
Republicans have largely retained their allegiance to Trump. Jim Jordan was selected as their next House leader, while John Thune retained Senate Republican leadership.

The central question: Can divided government produce meaningful economic reforms, or will confrontation dominate Washington?

🇺🇦 2. UKRAINE: PEACE TALKS CONTINUE AS CIVILIANS DIE

Russian attacks struck Zaporizhzhia and Odesa on November 13, killing at least three people and injuring dozens, according to Ukrainian officials. Residential buildings suffered serious damage.

Ukrainian drones also struck targets inside Russia, including energy infrastructure. Both countries continue attacking despite renewed diplomatic negotiations.
American envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner participated in efforts involving Moscow and Kyiv. Negotiations in Abu Dhabi produced agreement on a prisoner exchange but no settlement of fundamental territorial disagreements.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy demands security guarantees and protection of Ukrainian sovereignty. President Vladimir Putin maintains territorial and military demands Kyiv rejects.

Europe fears any agreement permitting territorial conquest could undermine continental security for generations.

🇵🇸 3. GAZA: A CEASEFIRE WITHOUT LASTING SECURITY

More than a year after the October 2025 ceasefire, Gaza continues experiencing deadly violence and humanitarian suffering.

An Israeli strike on Nasser Hospital's surgical wing killed six people, including a surgeon and a 13-year-old boy, according to Associated Press reporting.
Israel said it targeted a Hamas commander allegedly operating from the facility but did not publicly provide supporting evidence.

Gaza's hospitals face devastating shortages of medical equipment, medicine and functioning infrastructure.

International humanitarian law protects medical facilities, subject to narrowly defined exceptions and strict restrictions on attacks.

The challenge extends beyond ending hostilities: rebuilding healthcare, restoring homes and establishing legitimate, lasting security for Israelis and Palestinians.

🇮🇷 4. IRAN: GULF TENSIONS THREATEN INTERNATIONAL SHIPPING

The United States reported intercepting two Iranian drones approaching Bahrain. Iran claimed an attack against American radar facilities, which Washington disputed.

Military tensions surrounding Iran continue threatening shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a strategically critical international energy passage.
The United Nations maritime agency documented 134 regional maritime incidents by November 11, with deadly consequences for seafarers.

Renewed confrontation could disrupt energy supplies, increase transportation costs and further undermine regional stability.

💰 5. GLOBAL ECONOMY: INFLATION AND INTEREST RATES

American producer prices increased 6.5% over the year ending in October, reinforcing concerns about persistent inflation.

Federal Reserve officials are discussing additional interest-rate increases. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent argues that temporary energy-related price increases should not provoke excessive tightening, while other policymakers warn inflation has spread beyond energy.
Higher interest rates can restrain inflation but also increase borrowing costs for households, businesses and governments.

The consequences extend internationally through exchange rates, investment flows and the cost of financing development.

🤖 6. ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE: TECHNOLOGY MARKETS FACE UNCERTAINTY

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's unexpected resignation has unsettled investors in the semiconductor industry.

Technology stocks declined on November 13, with the Nasdaq falling approximately 0.9%. Investors are examining whether massive artificial-intelligence infrastructure spending can generate sustainable profits.
Anthropic's anticipated public offering could become another major test of confidence in the industry.

Beyond financial markets, governments face difficult questions about employment, cybersecurity, surveillance, misinformation and the concentration of technological power.

Innovation offers extraordinary possibilities, but responsible human oversight remains essential.

🌡️ 7. CLIMATE: WORLD LEADERS CONFRONT AN UNEQUAL CRISIS

At COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres called for drastic reductions in greenhouse gas emissions.

Negotiations remain divided over fossil fuels, financial assistance and responsibility for addressing climate damage.
Developing nations argue that wealthy industrialized countries should provide greater assistance because historical emissions helped create the problem.

A climate-finance commitment targets $300 billion annually for developing countries by 2035. Achieving meaningful reductions while protecting vulnerable economies remains a central challenge.

🇸🇩 8. SUDAN: WAR, DISPLACEMENT AND THE TRADE IN GOLD

Sudan's conflict, which began in April 2023, continues devastating communities and forcing millions from their homes.

A new Swissaid investigation alleges that illicit gold from conflict-affected countries continues entering the United Arab Emirates despite tighter regulations.
Researchers estimate that illicit gold imports into the UAE reached $74 billion in 2024, including substantial shipments originating in African countries.

The findings raise difficult questions about international supply chains and whether commercial profits are helping sustain armed conflicts.

🌎 9. THE BIGGER PICTURE: HUMANITY'S SHARED FUTURE

Today's developments reveal interconnected dangers.

War destabilizes trade. Energy disruptions intensify inflation. Climate disasters burden vulnerable societies. Technological advances challenge existing economic structures.
Yet diplomacy, scientific progress, humanitarian assistance and democratic institutions provide opportunities for constructive change.

FINAL ASSESSMENT

November 13, 2026, reveals a world confronting difficult choices rather than inevitable catastrophe.

The most important unresolved questions concern whether Ukraine's sovereignty can be protected through diplomacy, whether civilians in Gaza and Sudan can receive lasting protection, whether inflation can be contained without serious economic damage, and whether governments can cooperate on climate change.

The coming months will test not only international leadership, but humanity's willingness to place human dignity, justice and peaceful coexistence above narrow political and economic interests.

Sources: Reuters and Associated Press reporting, November 10–13, 2026; CBS News and ABC News election coverage; United Nations climate and humanitarian reporting; Swissaid investigation as reported by AP.

Reporting reflects information available November 13, 2026. Casualty figures and contested military claims may change as independent verification continues.

text:
Friday the 13th, November 2026. Friends and fellow citizens, take a look at what's happening around us.

America's aviation system experiences a nationwide ground stop following a telecommunications failure. DHS says a cyberattack has not been ruled out, although no evidence of one has been established.

Microsoft suffers a widespread outage affecting Outlook, Teams and other services. The company reports no indication of malicious activity.

NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang resigns amid investigations concerning a relationship with a woman suspected of Chinese intelligence ties. Huang has not been found guilty of espionage.

Elon Musk publicly says it would be an honor to hire Huang. Meanwhile, Ukraine reports that restrictions on SpaceX's Starshield service are interfering with drones used to defend against Russian attacks.

President Trump honored Huang at the White House in October. Reports say Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned Trump about intelligence concerns months earlier. Trump disputes that account.

Congress is now demanding records about NVIDIA's chip exports and national-security safeguards.

China seeks advanced American technology while Russia continues its war against Ukraine. Millions of Americans also have retirement savings exposed to technology companies through their 401(k)s.

Who knew what, when, and why? Are our institutions adequately protecting American interests?

These incidents have different causes, and no evidence establishes that they are part of one coordinated attack. But they raise important questions about foreign influence, national security, corporate responsibility and government accountability.

NOW CONSIDER GEORGE WASHINGTON'S WARNING.

In 1796, Washington opened his Farewell Address:

"Friends and Fellow-Citizens"

He explained that his concerns came from:

"a solicitude for your welfare which cannot end but with my life"

He warned about replacing the people's interests with:

"the will of a party, often a small but artful and enterprising minority"

He described the dangers of political passions creating:

"ill-founded jealousies and false alarms"

And he warned:

"It opens the door to foreign influence and corruption"

Washington also cautioned Americans:

"to guard against the impostures of pretended patriotism"

He believed:

"it is essential that public opinion should be enlightened."

Think about those words. Not through a Democrat's lens. Not through a Republican's lens. Through your own independent American lens.

How many warnings can you recognize in today's headlines?

Washington offered these warnings to protect our union, our liberties and future generations. He did not want Americans divided into enemies by political factions.

Our mission at The Higher Desires includes encouraging independent thought, peace, compassion and helping our fellow citizens.

The Senate continues reading Washington's Farewell Address near his birthday every year. Here is the February 2026 reading. Take the opportunity to listen and decide for yourself how much of his warning applies today.

GEORGE WASHINGTON'S FAREWELL ADDRESS:
https://t.co/7WU7S68cHS

AND NOW, A LITTLE GOOD NEWS!

If you're grounded, waiting for a flight or simply tired of the bad news, take a few minutes for some good-time rock and roll.

Today, Friday the 13th, The Higher Desires released "Clouds Roll By," a song made for having a good time and enjoying the moments life gives us.

Sometimes we all need to get away from the bad moments, even if only for a song, and let those troubles roll on by like a cloud.

All royalties earned from "Clouds Roll By" during 2026 are pledged to veterans' charities. Thank you to those who served and to everyone supporting independent music.

text:
WHO HAS THE RIGHT TO DESTROY WHAT SOMEONE ELSE HAS SPENT A LIFETIME BUILDING?

There is one question I simply cannot ignore.

How many of the people involved in deciding Jensen Huang’s future have ever built a company the size of NVIDIA?

How many have achieved technological breakthroughs of comparable magnitude?

How many have possessed the vision, determination, courage, and perseverance to invest decades of their lives in technologies that others could barely comprehend?

How many have even dared to dream of building something so extraordinary?

Perhaps some of them have achieved remarkable things in their respective fields. I would never deny that.

But there is a fundamental difference we must remember.

Investing money in a technological revolution is not the same as imagining it, designing it, building it, and turning it into reality.

Capital matters. Good governance matters. Boards of directors have legitimate responsibilities and must fulfill them.

But money does not automatically confer wisdom, human sensitivity, or an understanding of what it truly means to be a creator.

A company like NVIDIA was not born simply because someone signed a check.

It was born from a vision. From thousands of difficult decisions, extraordinary risks, sleepless nights, and the relentless dedication of people who dared to imagine a future that did not yet exist.

And now I ask:

What sense of security can any founder or executive have if their private life can become a weapon against them before any relevant wrongdoing has been proven?

Are we seriously suggesting that our greatest innovators should retreat into monasteries?

That they should never fall in love?

That they should never make mistakes in their personal relationships?

That they should give up their private lives out of fear that someone might use their feelings, relationships, or vulnerabilities to destroy their reputation?

For heaven’s sake, wake up!

Corporate security should protect industrial secrets, prevent conflicts of interest, and safeguard people against abuses of power.

It should not become a permanent system of moral surveillance over human intimacy.

Of course, extraordinary positions carry extraordinary responsibilities.

But they should also demand extraordinarily fair, rigorous, and proportionate procedures.

And if sufficient evidence does not exist to justify a decision of such magnitude, reconsidering that decision would not be a defeat.

It would be an act of intelligence, justice, courage, and respect.

Because there is something no stock market valuation can ever fully measure:

The decades of life, imagination, sacrifice, hope, and talent that a human being devotes to creating something that changes the world.

We can replace a position.

We can appoint another CEO.

We can restructure a board of directors.

But we cannot buy, with all the money in the world, the lifetime someone devoted to imagining the impossible and making it real.

And perhaps it is time we remembered that.

There is also another dimension that deserves far greater respect: human relationships.

Behind every public figure stands a private human being.

There may be a wife, a family, children, loved ones, personal commitments, difficult conversations, and emotions that outsiders cannot possibly understand in their entirety.

Those relationships belong first and foremost to the people directly involved.

Not to the media.

Not to strangers seeking entertainment.

Not to a public spectacle in which everyone suddenly believes they have the right to judge another person's most intimate decisions.

Love is not a crime. Human complexity is not evidence of guilt. And personal relationships should not automatically become matters of public prosecution.

If there is coercion, abuse of power, espionage, deliberate disclosure of confidential information, or another demonstrable violation, then investigate it and establish responsibility.

Absolutely.

But let us stop confusing suspicion with proof, personal morality with universal justice, and public curiosity with the right to invade someone's private life.

And let us ask another uncomfortable question.

If someone occupying a position of such strategic importance were unknowingly exposed to a genuine foreign intelligence threat, where would the preventive security and counterintelligence mechanisms be?

Would their responsibility not include identifying risks, issuing appropriate warnings, and protecting individuals and national interests before damage occurs?

Security should mean prevention and protection, not merely finding someone to blame after a controversy explodes.

If serious wrongdoing is not established, there are two paths worth considering.

The first is the path of institutional wisdom: reconsider the decision, offer a return where appropriate, reform the procedures that failed, and acknowledge any injustice.

And if an injustice has truly occurred, there is something remarkably simple that powerful institutions should never be too proud to do.

Apologize.

Yes. Apologize.

Not as a sign of weakness, but as a demonstration of greatness.

The second path is that Jensen Huang may decide to build something entirely new.

And imagine what could happen then.

Elon Musk, what if extraordinary minds joined forces to create a fundamentally new generation of computing?

Ternary architectures. Multi-valued transistors. Revolutionary memory systems. New approaches to energy efficiency and computational performance.

I have personally developed functional ternary implementations using CUDA. Moving those concepts into physical hardware and independently demonstrating measurable advantages would be the next great challenge.

The goal would not be to reproduce NVIDIA.

It would be to imagine what comes after NVIDIA.

But before we talk about processors, artificial intelligence, corporate valuations, or technological revolutions, we must remember something infinitely more important.

Jensen Huang is a human being.

Not merely a corporate asset.

Not a stock price.

Not a headline.

Not a disposable piece on someone else's chessboard.

A human being with a history, a family, relationships, responsibilities, hopes, and the same fundamental right to dignity and fairness as anyone else.

We can admire extraordinary achievements without placing anyone above accountability.

We can demand transparency without destroying reputations through speculation.

And we can protect national security without turning private human relationships into a public circus.

A civilization that demands its greatest creators behave like flawless machines, while proudly proclaiming its commitment to individual freedom, needs to confront its own contradictions.

This is not about demanding special privileges for powerful people.

It is about defending principles that belong to everyone, from the humblest worker to the founder of a global technology leader:

The right to dignity. The right to privacy. The right to a fair investigation. And the right not to be condemned by rumors.

Because if we lose those principles, we may succeed in building the most advanced processors in the universe while failing at something infinitely more fundamental.

Our own humanity.

The future does not merely need more powerful machines. It needs wiser minds, greater compassion, and the courage to distinguish justice from prejudice.

And perhaps the greatest revolution of all will begin when we finally learn that technological progress means very little unless human dignity advances alongside it.

With respect for Jensen Huang, his family, everyone involved, and all those who have dedicated their lives to creating a better future.

A heartfelt embrace, from the depths of my soul.

— Atlas Azul

text:
MIT Technology Review’s What’s Next series looks across industries, trends, and technologies to give you a first look at the future. You can read the rest of our series here.

This time last year we did something reckless. In an industry where nothing stands still, we had a go at predicting the future. 

How did we do? Our four big bets for 2023 were that the next big thing in chatbots would be multimodal (check: the most powerful large language models out there, OpenAI’s GPT-4 and Google DeepMind’s Gemini, work with text, images and audio); that policymakers would draw up tough new regulations (check: Biden’s executive order came out in October and the European Union’s AI Act was finally agreed in December); Big Tech would feel pressure from open-source startups (half right: the open-source boom continues, but AI companies like OpenAI and Google DeepMind still stole the limelight); and that AI would change big pharma for good (too soon to tell: the AI revolution in drug discovery is in full swing, but the first drugs developed using AI are still some years from market).

Now we’re doing it again.

We decided to ignore the obvious. We know that large language models will continue to dominate. Regulators will grow bolder. AI’s problems—from bias to copyright to doomerism—will shape the agenda for researchers, regulators, and the public, not just in 2024 but for years to come. (Read more about our six big questions for generative AI here.)

Instead, we’ve picked a few more specific trends. Here’s what to watch out for in 2024. (Come back next year and check how we did.)

1

Customized chatbots

You get a chatbot! And you get a chatbot! In 2024, tech companies that invested heavily in generative AI will be under pressure to prove that they can make money off their products. To do this, AI giants Google and OpenAI are betting big on going small: both are developing user-friendly platforms that allow people to customize powerful language models and make their own mini chatbots that cater to their specific needs—no coding skills required. Both have launched web-based tools that allow anyone to become a generative-AI app developer. 

In 2024, generative AI might actually become useful for the regular, non-tech person, and we are going to see more people tinkering with a million little AI models. State-of-the-art AI models, such as GPT-4 and Gemini, are multimodal, meaning they can process not only text but images and even videos. This new capability could unlock a whole bunch of new apps. For example, a real estate agent can upload text from previous listings, fine-tune a powerful model to generate similar text with just a click of a button, upload videos and photos of new listings, and simply ask the customized AI to generate a description of the property. 

But of course, the success of this plan hinges on whether these models work reliably. Language models often make stuff up, and generative models are riddled with biases. They are also easy to hack, especially if they are allowed to browse the web. Tech companies have not solved any of these problems. When the novelty wears off, they’ll have to offer their customers ways to deal with these problems. 

—Melissa Heikkilä

2

Generative AI’s second wave will be video

It’s amazing how fast the fantastic becomes familiar. The first generative models to produce photorealistic images exploded into the mainstream in 2022—and soon became commonplace. Tools like OpenAI’s DALL-E, Stability AI’s Stable Diffusion, and Adobe’s Firefly flooded the internet with jaw-dropping images of everything from the pope in Balenciaga to prize-winning art. But it’s not all good fun: for every pug waving pompoms, there’s another piece of knock-off fantasy art or sexist sexual stereotyping.

The new frontier is text-to-video. Expect it to take everything that was good, bad, or ugly about text-to-image and supersize it.

A year ago we got the first glimpse of what generative models could do when they were trained to stitch together multiple still images into clips a few seconds long. The results were distorted and jerky. But the tech has rapidly improved.

Runway, a startup that makes generative video models (and the company that co-created Stable Diffusion), is dropping new versions of its tools every few months. Its latest model, called Gen-2, still generates video just a few seconds long, but the quality is striking. The best clips aren’t far off what Pixar might put out.

Runway has set up an annual AI film festival that showcases experimental movies made with a range of AI tools. This year’s festival has a $60,000 prize pot, and the 10 best films will be screened in New York and Los Angeles.

It’s no surprise that top studios are taking notice. Movie giants, including Paramount and Disney, are now exploring the use of generative AI throughout their production pipeline. The tech is being used to lip-sync actors’ performances to multiple foreign-language overdubs. And it is reinventing what’s possible with special effects. In 2023, Indiana Jones and the Dial of Destiny starred a de-aged deepfake Harrison Ford. This is just the start.  

Away from the big screen, deepfake tech for marketing or training purposes is taking off too. For example, UK-based Synthesia makes tools that can turn a one-off performance by an actor into an endless stream of deepfake avatars, reciting whatever script you give them at the push of a button. According to the company, its tech is now used by 44% of Fortune 100 companies. 

The ability to do so much with so little raises serious questions for actors. Concerns about studios’ use and misuse of AI were at the heart of the SAG-AFTRA strikes last year. But the true impact of the tech is only just becoming apparent. “The craft of filmmaking is fundamentally changing,” says Souki Mehdaoui, an independent filmmaker and cofounder of Bell & Whistle, a consultancy specializing in creative technologies.

—Will Douglas Heaven

3

AI-generated election disinformation will be everywhere 

If recent elections are anything to go by, AI-generated election disinformation and deepfakes are going to be a huge problem as a record number of people march to the polls in 2024. We’re already seeing politicians weaponizing these tools. In Argentina, two presidential candidates created AI-generated images and videos of their opponents to attack them. In Slovakia, deepfakes of a liberal pro-European party leader threatening to raise the price of beer and making jokes about child pornography spread like wildfire during the country’s elections. And in the US, Donald Trump has cheered on a group that uses AI to generate memes with racist and sexist tropes. 

While it’s hard to say how much these examples have influenced the outcomes of elections, their proliferation is a worrying trend. It will become harder than ever to recognize what is real online. In an already inflamed and polarized political climate, this could have severe consequences.

Just a few years ago creating a deepfake would have required advanced technical skills, but generative AI has made it stupidly easy and accessible, and the outputs are looking increasingly realistic. Even reputable sources might be fooled by AI-generated content. For example, users-submitted AI-generated images purporting to depict the Israel-Gaza crisis have flooded stock image marketplaces like Adobe’s. 

The coming year will be pivotal for those fighting against the proliferation of such content. Techniques to track and mitigate it content are still in early days of development. Watermarks, such as Google DeepMind’s SynthID, are still mostly voluntary and not completely foolproof. And social media platforms are notoriously slow in taking down misinformation. Get ready for a massive real-time experiment in busting AI-generated fake news. 

—Melissa Heikkilä

4

Robots that multitask

Inspired by some of the core techniques behind generative AI’s current boom, roboticists are starting to build more general-purpose robots that can do a wider range of tasks.

The last few years in AI have seen a shift away from using multiple small models, each trained to do different tasks—identifying images, drawing them, captioning them—toward single, monolithic models trained to do all these things and more. By showing OpenAI’s GPT-3 a few additional examples (known as fine-tuning), researchers can train it to solve coding problems, write movie scripts, pass high school biology exams, and so on. Multimodal models, like GPT-4 and Google DeepMind’s Gemini, can solve visual tasks as well as linguistic ones.

The same approach can work for robots, so it wouldn’t be necessary to train one to flip pancakes and another to open doors: a one-size-fits-all model could give robots the ability to multitask. Several examples of work in this area emerged in 2023.

In June, DeepMind released Robocat (an update on last year’s Gato), which generates its own data from trial and error to learn how to control many different robot arms (instead of one specific arm, which is more typical). 

In October, the company put out yet another general-purpose model for robots, called RT-X, and a big new general-purpose training data set, in collaboration with 33 university labs. Other top research teams, such as RAIL (Robotic Artificial Intelligence and Learning) at the University of California, Berkeley, are looking at similar tech.

The problem is a lack of data. Generative AI draws on an internet-size data set of text and images. In comparison, robots have very few good sources of data to help them learn how to do many of the industrial or domestic tasks we want them to.

Lerrel Pinto at New York University leads one team addressing that. He and his colleagues are developing techniques that let robots learn by trial and error, coming up with their own training data as they go. In an even more low-key project, Pinto has recruited volunteers to collect video data from around their homes using an iPhone camera mounted to a trash picker. Big companies have also started to release large data sets for training robots in the last couple of years, such as Meta’s Ego4D.

This approach is already showing promise in driverless cars. Startups such as Wayve, Waabi, and Ghost are pioneering a new wave of self-driving AI that uses a single large model to control a vehicle rather than multiple smaller models to control specific driving tasks. This has let small companies catch up with giants like Cruise and Waymo. Wayve is now testing its driverless cars on the narrow, busy streets of London. Robots everywhere are set to get a similar boost.

—Will Douglas Heaven

Amazon ($AMZN) has revived a deal with Fermi, the struggling Texas data-center developer co-founded by former U.S. Energy Secretary Rick Perry. Fermi announced a 600MW agreement with an unnamed hyperscaler identified by the FT as Amazon, nearly a year after their previous talks collapsed.

* Deal Terms: Amazon is expected to build its own data centers at Fermi's Amarillo campus, beginning in 2027. The arrangement includes a $200M construction prepayment, a signed $15M pre-construction agreement and another $90M for materials still being finalized.
* Financing & Deadlines: Fermi plans to begin construction by December 1 but must secure financing and a definitive tenant agreement for at least 200MW by December 31 to satisfy conditions of its 99-year Texas Tech University land lease.
* Infrastructure: Fermi reports 6GW of air permits, five gas turbines, 4.6 miles of gas pipelines, 300 prepared acres and 220,000 MMBtu in gas commitments. Its permits face legal challenges, while Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has pledged a moratorium on new approvals.
* Financial Pressure: Fermi reported a $141.6M Q3 net loss, $286.3M in cash and roughly $958M in debt. Its $6.5B agreement with neocloud Tensorwave also collapsed.
* Previous Setbacks: Amazon withdrew a $150M investment, Oracle negotiations faltered, and co-founder Toby Neugebauer was ousted amid disputed misconduct allegations and a boardroom battle. Fermi lost over 80% of its peak valuation, which exceeded $19B after its 2025 IPO.

text:
How AI Will Replace Primary Care: A Timeline

I predict in 20 years AI will be the end of primary care as it exists today.

I'm a primary care physician myself. For 25 years I have treated patients on three continents. Things are changing fast.

Here is my timeline -

Now to 2028:
Physicians Adapt AI

Doctors adopt AI first, using it for hard cases, prior auths, patient notes, etc. Trust in AI starts. AI takes the paperwork nobody likes. The market stays fragmented, one tool per task, while foundation models like GPT, Claude, and Gemini become healthcare’s operating system as they get stronger.

2028 to 2032:
Patients Adapt AI

Utah has AI renewing prescriptions today. The UAE recently approved a law governing AI across its health sector, covering safety standards, liability, and patient rights. Medical boards push back, arguing medicine needs humans. Patients choose the faster and more convenient path. Fewer graduates choose primary care, and the shortage worsens.

2032 to 2036:
The Reckoning

An AI system harms a patient badly. Doctors make mistakes too, but the AI’s mistake becomes the catalyst for oversight. Regulation follows fast: federal standards, licensing frameworks, clear liability. Accuracy, security, and privacy all strengthen. AI health companies get malpractice insurance.

2036 to 2040:
Healthcare Consolidation

Fragmentation resolves as AI improves. Full primary care platforms emerge: triage, chronic disease management, prescriptions, mental health, labs, etc.. Insurers build reimbursement codes. Public sentiment flips. What felt experimental in 2026 feels routine by 2036, following online banking's journey.

2040 to 2046:
The New Standard

Primary care runs through AI platforms first, monitored by medical boards. Doctors remain, but focus on complex cases and the human presence when autopilot fails. Industrialized countries move first, with select parts of AI-care arriving in lower-GDP nations.

20 years is a guess. Pioneering Concierge Medicine and Direct Primary Care taught me healthcare takes about 20 years to change.

But people are desperate.

Nearly 1 in 3 American adults has no primary care home.

More than 100 million Americans face barriers to access.

Worldwide, 4.6 billion people lack access to essential health services.

Autonomous NPs and PAs alone will fall short.

Urgent care and ER visits for primary care will become unsustainable.

Doctors will choose specialties over primary care as they have been.

There's debate that AI has no empathy, or that AI models lack a relationship.

Empathy can be taught to AI, just as we were taught in med school.

10 minute visits every four months doesn't build a relationship, sorry. It build frustration.

Primary care is already disappearing, and people are struggling for access that will continue to worsen.

This storm has been brewing for decades.

Noah built the ark before the storm.

At ASTRID, that's precisely what we're doing.

We're building that ark.

text:
The Night Watchman's Time Slip: How Leo Frank Was Accused of Framing Newt Lee

Newt Lee's Testimony at the Leo Frank Murder Trial, as Reported by The Atlanta Georgian, July 28–31, 1913

Newt Lee Takes the Stand at Leo Frank's Trial

On Monday, July 28, 1913, Newt Lee testified in Fulton County Superior Court at the murder trial of Leo Max Frank, superintendent of Atlanta's National Pencil Company.

Three months earlier, Lee had discovered 13-year-old Mary Phagan's body in the factory basement and immediately called the police. Instead of remaining solely a witness, he was arrested and held in the Fulton County Tower.

Judge Leonard S. Roan presided. Solicitor General Hugh Manson Dorsey led the prosecution, assisted by Frank Arthur Hooper. Frank's defense attorneys included Luther Zeigler Rosser, Reuben R. Arnold, and Herbert Haas.

Mary Phagan's mother, Mrs. J. W. Coleman, testified first, followed by George W. Epps. Newton Lee was the third witness.

The Atlanta Georgian reported that Lee repeated his account of discovering the body and described Frank's unusual conduct on the afternoon of the murder. On July 29, the newspaper featured Lee's testimony and Rosser's lengthy cross-examination.

Lee endured approximately four hours and forty minutes of questioning. Although Rosser exposed differences between his trial testimony and earlier statements, the Georgian reported that the defense failed to obtain admissions directly implicating him in the murder (AG, July 28–29, 1913).

Lee Warns That Leo Frank Is Trying to Blame Him

The possibility of a frame-up had been raised months before the trial.

On Wednesday, April 30, 1913, The Atlanta Georgian published an article titled "Looks Like Frank Is Trying to Put Crime on Me, Says Lee."

The newspaper quoted Lee:

"It looks like Mr. Frank was trying to put the crime on me" (AG, April 30, 1913).

Lee had endured intensive questioning while maintaining that he knew nothing about Mary Phagan's murder beyond discovering her body.

His concern centered on Frank's changing account of the factory's mechanical time clock. Frank initially declared Lee's half-hour punches correct but subsequently reported that several were missing. It was a Sunday to Monday, flip flop. 

The consequences were serious. A properly punched record supported Lee's claim that he remained on duty. Missing intervals could suggest he had enough time to leave the factory, travel home, change clothing, and return. The whole going home thing was to suggest he might be hiding evidence there. 

This contradiction became central to the prosecution's argument that Frank was attempting to direct suspicion toward the watchman. There were notes pointing to the watchman, there was a blood soaked shirt pointing to the watchman, and there was a timeslip pointing to the watchman. 

Frank's Unusual Instructions on April 26

Lee testified that Frank instructed him on Friday, April 25, to report at 4 p.m. Saturday instead of his regular 6 p.m. starting time.

Saturday was Confederate Memorial Day, a Georgia state holiday. Frank had a date with his Christian brother-in-law to go watch the ball game featuring the Atlanta crackers.

When Lee arrived, he found the street entrance unlocked but the interior doors secured. Frank emerged from his office, rubbing his hands, apologized for summoning him early, and sent him away until 6 p.m.

Lee considered this unusual. He walked around downtown Atlanta, watched a medicine seller entertaining a crowd, and returned as instructed.

Frank then told him not to punch the clock immediately because the recording paper needed to be replaced.

The Georgian quoted Lee's description of Frank handling the paper:

"He sort of fumbled it" (AG, July 28, 1913).

Frank controlled the recording mechanism, making his handling of the paper significant when investigators later questioned its accuracy.

Shortly afterward, former bookkeeper James Milton Gantt arrived to retrieve shoes. Lee thought Frank appeared surprised and frightened when Gantt arrived.

Later that evening, Frank telephoned to ask whether everything was all right. Lee testified that Frank had never personally called him during a shift before.

These events did not establish wrongdoing, but they gave investigators reasons to question Frank's movements and behavior.

Sunday, April 27: Frank Declares the Time Slip Correct

The most significant evidence concerning Lee's time record emerged from former county policeman W. W. "Boots" Rogers.

On Wednesday, July 30, The Atlanta Georgian published "Gantt Has Startling Evidence; Dorsey Promises New Testimony Against Frank," featuring the subheading "State Adds New Link to Evidence Chain by Boots Rogers' Story."

Rogers accompanied officers who brought Frank to the factory after Lee discovered Mary Phagan's body early Sunday morning, April 27, 1913.

Frank unlocked the time clock and removed Lee's recording slip that morning.

Those identified as present included Frank, Newt Lee, factory foreman N. V. Darley, and Woods White "Boots" Rogers. Other officers were involved in the factory investigation. Lee was handcuffed and stood near Rogers.

Rogers testified that Frank examined the slip and declared:

"They are all punched all right" (AG, July 30, 1913).

Lee had given essentially the same account during his July 28 testimony.

Rogers also examined the paper and saw no obvious missing punches. He recalled the first at approximately 6:01 p.m. and the second at 6:32 p.m.

Frank then wrote April 26, 1913, on the paper, folded it, and carried it into his office.

This detail was significant. The superintendent had personally removed the original recording slip, declared it satisfactory, and taken possession of it.

If the record later appeared irregular, investigators needed to establish whether the paper remained unchanged and who handled it afterward (AG, July 30, 1–2).

Monday, April 28: Frank's Account Changes

The following day, according to Lee's earlier inquest testimony, Frank described the clock record differently.

Lee stated that Frank had told him Sunday morning he had missed no punches, but by Monday morning said the clock had not been punched correctly.

The later trial testimony complicated the exact timing.

On July 30, Detective John R. Black testified that Frank first told him about the irregularities on Tuesday, April 29. Black also acknowledged that the original slip had been delivered to Chief of Detectives Newport A. Lanford on Monday.

Lee therefore placed Frank's changed account on Monday, while Black recalled hearing about the discrepancies Tuesday.

Regardless of the precise hour, the contradiction remained: Frank initially pronounced the slip correct and later identified missing or irregular intervals that could implicate Lee.

Contemporary reports described three irregular periods, including substantial gaps during the evening and early morning.

Frank's defense argued that he had initially checked whether the numbered positions were punched without carefully examining the elapsed time between them.

That explanation was possible. A slip could contain a punch at every numbered position while still recording irregular intervals.

But the discrepancy, combined with Frank's access to the clock, justified examining the original paper and its custody.

Frank Says Lee Had Time to Go Home and Return

The importance of the missing punches became clearer during Detective Black's trial testimony.

Dorsey questioned Black about Frank's suggestion that the irregularities gave Lee enough time to travel home and return to the factory.

Black attributed that statement to Frank after he examined the recording slip again.

This was more serious than simply identifying a mechanical irregularity. Frank had suggested a possible explanation for Lee's whereabouts during the missing intervals.

That explanation became especially damaging when detectives searched Lee's residence and discovered a bloodstained shirt.

The prosecution argued that Frank's changing interpretation of the clock helped direct suspicion toward the watchman.

Black's recollection of the exact chronology was challenged by Rosser, but Frank's statement about Lee having time to go home became a significant part of Dorsey's attempted frame-up argument.

Could the Clock Have Been Manipulated?

On July 29, The Atlanta Georgian reported testimony from City Detective J. M. Starnes concerning an experiment with the factory clock.

Officer Starnes watched a replacement night watchman produce an entire twelve-hour series of punches in approximately five minutes.

The experiment demonstrated that someone familiar with the mechanism could rapidly manufacture a series of clock punches.

It did not establish that Frank altered Lee's slip. But it showed that the mechanical record was not automatically reliable proof of a watchman's actual movements.

The prosecution argued that Frank might have manipulated the evidence to incriminate Lee. Frank denied altering it.

The unresolved questions concerned who possessed the original slip, whether anyone changed its markings, and why Frank's interpretation differed between Sunday and the following days (AG, July 29, 1913).

The Bloodstained Shirt Found at Lee's Home

The second suspicious item was a linen shirt discovered in a trash barrel at Lee's residence on Henry Street.

Detectives John R. Black and Fred Bullard found the garment beneath discarded clothing. It carried conspicuous bloodstains. The shirt did not have an "African scent" of foul body odor. It looked like someone dipped the shirt in blood on both sides. And the shirt looked like it was cleanly laundered. The conclusion of investigators is that it was a contrived plant that had been staged to incriminate Newt Lee.

Lee acknowledged that it resembled one of his old shirts but denied wearing it around the time of Mary Phagan's murder.

He maintained that he had not seen it for approximately two years.

The shirt appeared to support the theory that the missing clock punches gave Lee enough time to travel home, change clothing, and return. In fact, Leo Frank stated that it did so. 

But there was no eyewitness testimony establishing that Lee wore the garment on April 26.

Its physical condition also raised serious doubts.

Why the Shirt Appeared to Be Planted

On Thursday, July 31, The Atlanta Georgian reported testimony from Atlanta City Bacteriologist Dr. Claude A. Smith.

Smith believed the blood had been deposited while the shirt was not being worn.

He described the garment as apparently clean apart from the blood, without ordinary signs of recent use around the collar and armpits.

Blood appeared on the inside and had soaked outward through the fabric.

Smith believed the garment might have been used to wipe up blood rather than worn during a struggle.

These observations weakened the accusation that Lee had worn the shirt while murdering Mary Phagan.

They raised the possibility that someone had deliberately stained an unused garment and placed it among Lee's discarded clothing.

The examination did not establish who applied the blood or placed the shirt in the barrel. Nevertheless, its condition gave prosecutors grounds to suspect planted evidence (AG, July 31, 1913).

The Atlanta Georgian Reports Dorsey's Accusation

On July 31, The Atlanta Georgian carried the front-page headline:

"'Plant' Charged By State Against Newt Lee."

The newspaper reported Dorsey's allegation that the bloodstained shirt had been deliberately placed at Lee's residence to shift suspicion away from Frank.

Dorsey connected the discovery with an earlier request by Frank's attorney Herbert Haas that detectives search Frank's home.

According to the prosecution's theory, detectives would find nothing incriminating at Frank's residence and then turn toward Lee's, where the bloodstained garment would be discovered.

The missing clock punches supplied the apparent reason Lee might have gone home.

Dorsey's argument was that these events were connected rather than unrelated coincidences.

It was an accusation presented during the trial, not proof identifying the person who planted the garment (AG, July 31, 1).

Attorney and Bnai Brith member, Herbert Haas, and His Legal Defense of Frank

Detective Black testified that Haas requested a police search of Frank's residence after appearing at headquarters with Luther Rosser on Monday, April 28.

Detectives subsequently examined Frank's home and soiled laundry.

Frank later credited Rosser with insisting on the clothing inspection, while Black attributed the home-search request to Haas.

Dorsey argued that these actions helped guide investigators away from Frank and toward Lee.

Rosser countered by aggressively questioning Black about the chronology of the investigation.

The Georgian reported that Rosser exposed inconsistencies concerning when Frank identified missing punches and when detectives searched Lee's residence.

Black acknowledged confusion over parts of the timeline.

That weakened the precision of the prosecution's argument. But it did not establish that the shirt was genuine evidence against Lee or resolve Frank's conflicting statements about the time slip.

The Murder Notes Pointing Toward Lee

The third suspicious item consisted of two handwritten notes discovered near Mary Phagan's body.

They contained unusual spelling, confused language, and references suggesting that a Black night watchman was responsible.

Lee occupied that position at the factory.

Early handwriting examiners believed samples of his writing resembled the notes, making him appear even more suspicious.

Later in May, Jim Conley, another factory employee, admitted writing them.

Conley alleged that Frank instructed him to prepare the notes. Frank denied the accusation and maintained that Conley committed the murder.

Conley's admission undermined the handwriting identification of Lee.

The prosecution argued that the notes were intended to divert suspicion toward the watchman, although Frank's alleged role in their preparation remained disputed.

Rosser Tries to Turn the Notes Against Lee

During the July 29 trial proceedings, defense attorney Reuben Arnold argued that Lee's reaction to the notes revealed suspicious knowledge.

Rosser joined the argument, and Judge Roan permitted questioning about whether Lee appeared frightened when references to the night watchman were discussed.

Lee denied the incriminating statement attributed to him.

He maintained that someone was attempting to place responsibility for the murder upon him.

The defense's interpretation was questionable because Conley eventually admitted writing the notes.

Lee's recognition that the notes could implicate him did not establish that he wrote them or participated in the murder.

Rosser's Lengthy Cross-Examination

The Atlanta Georgian reported that Rosser spent approximately four hours and forty minutes challenging Lee's account.

Rosser questioned his movements, the discovery of Mary Phagan's body, the basement lighting, Frank's behavior when James Milton Gantt arrived, and the handling of the recording paper.

Lee resisted attempts to change his story, sometimes disputing the accuracy of earlier stenographic records.

On July 30, The Atlanta Georgian published James B. Nevin's column, "Rosser's Examination of Lee Just a Shot in Dark; Hoped to Start Quarry."

Nevin acknowledged Rosser's courtroom skill but questioned whether the questioning had established anything substantial against Lee.

The contrast was substantial. Frank had experienced attorneys challenging every inconsistency. Lee was a Black workingman who had discovered the body, summoned police, and remained imprisoned without being indicted.

The newspaper's treatment of Lee also reflected the racial attitudes of 1913 Atlanta. Some reports described his testimony through racial stereotypes, while others acknowledged that the defense had failed to obtain a direct admission of guilt.

Frank's Private Conversation With Lee

Another disturbing part of Lee's testimony concerned a private conversation arranged by detectives at police headquarters.

Lee said he was handcuffed to a chair when Frank entered.

He complained about being detained for something he knew nothing about.

According to Lee, Frank warned that continuing with the same account could bring serious consequences for both men.

The Atlanta Georgian of July 28 recorded Lee's allegation:

"if you keep that up, we both will go to hell" (AG, July 28, 1913).

Frank maintained that detectives had instructed him to question Lee privately.

The conversation remained disputed, but Lee's account raised a question: why would his continued insistence that he knew nothing about the murder create trouble for Frank?

Frank's Later Explanation and Lee's Release

In his August 1913 trial statement, Frank denied manipulating the time record. He also alleged that someone had partially erased markings he placed on the original recording slip.

The Atlanta Georgian reported this allegation on August 18.

That claim introduced another question about the paper's custody but did not establish who, if anyone, had changed it.

Newt Lee was never indicted for Mary Phagan's murder.

After Frank's conviction on Monday, August 25, 1913, Lee was released from the Fulton County Tower the following day, August 26, after approximately four months in custody.

The Georgian reported that he collected his belongings before leaving. His imprisonment had cost him his home, and he needed employment.

Lee's release ended his detention but could not erase the consequences of being suspected of murdering the child whose body he had discovered.

Conclusion: Three Pieces of Evidence and the Attempted Frame-Up

The testimony reported by The Atlanta Georgian raises serious questions about Frank's conduct toward Newt Lee.

This is what changed the tide of the case as it unfolded like this:

On Sunday, April 27, Frank examined the watchman's time slip in the presence of Lee, W. W. Rogers, and N. V. Darley and declared the punches correct.

On Monday, according to Lee's earlier testimony, Frank described the record as irregular. Detective Black later recalled hearing about the discrepancies Tuesday.

Frank subsequently suggested that the missing intervals allowed Lee enough time to travel home and return.

Detectives searched Lee's residence and found a bloodstained shirt whose condition suggested it had been stained while unworn.

Two murder notes appeared to implicate a Black night watchman, although Jim Conley admitted writing them.

The prosecution argued that Frank attempted to frame Lee through these three items.

The notes suggested whom investigators should suspect. The clock created an apparent opportunity. The shirt offered seemingly physical evidence.

The surviving record does not conclusively establish that Frank altered the recording slip, planted the shirt, or ordered Conley to write notes implicating Lee.

Nevertheless, these accusations were openly examined during the 1913 investigation and murder trial.

The Georgian preserved Lee's own warning that Frank appeared to be trying to put the crime on him, testimony concerning the Sunday approval of the time slip, and Dorsey's subsequent allegation that the bloodstained shirt had been planted.

Lee discovered Mary Phagan's body and summoned the police. He then spent four months imprisoned while investigators considered evidence that might have made him responsible for her murder.

The central historical question remains whether those three suspicious items were unrelated discoveries, mistakes, or parts of an effort to make the night watchman take the blame.

The historical focus is Newt Lee, the Black night watchman who discovered Mary Phagan's body, and the evidence behind the prosecution's accusation that Leo Frank attempted to frame him through three suspicious items: a disputed time slip, a bloodstained shirt, and two handwritten murder notes.

Leo Frank's Manufactured Murderer: The Attempt to Frame Newt Lee

Newt Lee at the Coroner's Inquest | The Atlanta Journal | Friday, May 9, 1913 | Atlanta, Georgia

The Night Watchman Who Became a Murder Suspect

On Friday, May 9, 1913, The Atlanta Journal published detailed accounts of the final coroner's inquest into the murder of 13-year-old Mary Phagan. Among the principal witnesses was Newt Lee, the Black night watchman who discovered her body in the basement of the National Pencil Company factory at 37 to 41 South Forsyth Street early Sunday, April 27.

Lee had telephoned police and led officers to the body. Yet within days, the man who reported the murder became a suspect, facing three pieces of potentially incriminating evidence: a disputed time-clock record, a blood-soaked shirt discovered at his residence, and two handwritten murder notes that appeared to point toward a Black man associated with the factory's night watch.

These objects later became central to the prosecution's argument that factory superintendent Leo Max Frank attempted to frame Lee. Particularly suspicious was Frank's changing account of the time slip, which he initially described as satisfactory before identifying gaps that supposedly gave the watchman enough time to travel home and return.

The May 9 Journal documented Lee's testimony, the detectives' findings, and serious questions about the conduct of Frank and his legal defense team (AJ, 6).

The Coroner's Inquest at Atlanta Police Headquarters

Fulton County Coroner Paul Donehoo conducted the inquest. His six-man jury initially assembled on Monday, April 28, at P. J. Bloomfield's undertaking establishment on South Pryor Street.

Later testimony was heard behind closed doors in the office of the Board of Police Commissioners at Atlanta police headquarters. The final session took place Thursday, May 8.

The jurors were foreman Homer C. Ashford, L. Glenn Dewberry, J. C. Hood, Clarence A. Langford, John Miller, and C. Y. Sheats.

Principal witnesses included Newt Lee, Leo Frank, Pinkerton investigator Harry Scott, city detective John R. Black, and factory official Herbert Schiff. Other leading figures included Chief of Detectives Newport Alonzo Lanford, Solicitor General Hugh Manson Dorsey, and Frank's attorneys Luther Zeigler Rosser and Herbert J. Haas.

Lee was questioned about his movements on April 26, his conversations with Frank, the factory time clock, and the bloody shirt discovered at his residence. He continued to deny involvement in Mary Phagan's murder (AJ, 6).

Frank Orders Lee to Arrive Two Hours Early

Lee ordinarily began work at 6 p.m. On Friday, April 25, Frank instructed him to report at 4 p.m. the following afternoon, Confederate Memorial Day, a Georgia state holiday.

When Lee arrived Saturday, he found the street entrance unlocked but the interior double doors locked, an unusual condition. Frank emerged from his private office, rubbing his hands, and unexpectedly told Lee to leave until 6 p.m.

Lee complained that he needed sleep, but Frank encouraged him to go out and enjoy himself.

Why would Frank instruct Lee to arrive two hours early, only to send him away?

One theory is that Frank wanted the watchman absent from the building. The defense could argue that Frank had simply changed his plans, but Lee's testimony established that his two-hour absence resulted from his employer's instructions (AJ, 6).

First Piece of Evidence: The Time Card

Saturday: Frank Handles the Clock

When Lee returned shortly before 6 p.m., Frank stopped him from punching the mechanical time clock while he installed a new paper recording slip.

The clock registered the watchman's rounds at approximately half-hour intervals. A complete record would support Lee's account of remaining on duty. Missing punches could suggest unexplained absences.

Frank's access to the mechanism became significant when the record was subsequently used against Lee (AJ, 6).

Sunday: Frank Says the Time Slip Is All Right

After Lee discovered Mary Phagan's body, police returned to the factory with Frank.

Frank opened the time clock and examined Lee's recording slip. William W. Rogers, known as Boots Rogers, also inspected it.

According to Rogers's testimony, Frank reported that the punches appeared satisfactory. Rogers likewise recalled seeing a punch corresponding to every numbered position.

Frank then installed another slip. The original record was not immediately secured under uninterrupted police custody.

The first inspection appeared to support Lee's account that he had made his rounds throughout the night (AJ, May 8, 1).

Monday: Frank Reports Missing Punches

By Monday, April 28, Frank was reporting discrepancies involving several missed half-hour punches.

One apparent gap extended from approximately 9:32 to 10:29 p.m. Other irregularities appeared around 11 p.m. and between approximately 2 and 3 a.m.

On Sunday, Frank said Lee's time slip was all right. By Monday, he was identifying missing punches that could implicate the watchman.

Frank explained that the first inspection had been superficial and that he had checked for marks without calculating every interval.

However, Lee insisted he had made his rounds regularly, and the handling of the original paper remained disputed.

No witness directly established that Frank altered the record, but the reversal in its interpretation created an opportunity to direct suspicion toward Lee (AJ, May 8, 1; AJ, July 31).

Frank Says Lee Had Time to Go Home and Return

During Frank's trial on Thursday, July 31, Detective John R. Black testified that Frank had remarked that the gaps in Lee's time record gave him sufficient time to leave the factory, travel home, and return during the night.

This statement connected the disputed time slip with the subsequent search of Lee's residence.

If investigators accepted the missing punches as evidence that Lee had abandoned his duties, they could argue that he went home to change bloodstained clothing before returning to the factory.

Under questioning by Solicitor General Hugh Manson Dorsey, Black testified that police searched Lee's residence after Frank directed attention to the discrepancies.

Frank's attorney Luther Zeigler Rosser challenged Black's recollection and exposed uncertainty about the timing of several conversations. Nevertheless, Black maintained that Frank's statements concerning the time record had influenced the investigation of Lee (AJ, July 31).

Second Piece of Evidence: The Blood-Soaked Shirt

Detectives Search Lee's Residence

On Tuesday, April 29, Detectives John R. Black and Fred Bullard searched Lee's residence at 40 Henry Street.

At the May 8 coroner's inquest, Black testified that they discovered a heavily bloodstained shirt near the bottom of a clothes barrel, covered by discarded garments.

The shirt differed from the clothing Lee wore when police first encountered him.

Lee could not positively identify it. He explained that a woman had made several shirts for him and that, if the bloody garment was store-bought, it was not one of those shirts.

Pinkerton investigator Harry Scott testified that Lee said he had not worn the garment for approximately two years.

No witness established that Lee wore it during Mary Phagan's murder (AJ, May 9, 6).

The Laboratory Examination Raises Doubts

Atlanta city bacteriologist Dr. Claude A. Smith examined the shirt.

The Atlanta Journal reported on Thursday, May 8, that the stains appeared relatively recent and probably consisted of human blood.

But Smith's findings suggested that the shirt had not been worn since being washed. The blood appeared to have been deposited while the garment was unworn, possibly by applying blood to it or using it to wipe up blood.

This weakened the theory that Lee had worn the shirt during the killing.

Smith could not identify who deposited the blood or placed the garment in the barrel. Nevertheless, his findings raised the possibility that someone had deliberately stained the shirt and planted it among Lee's discarded clothing (AJ, May 8, 8–9).

Herbert Haas Demands a Search of Frank's Home

Frank's attorney Herbert J. Haas became another figure in the prosecution's attempted-frame-up argument.

During the July 31 trial, Detective Black testified that Frank arrived at police headquarters on Monday, April 28, and consulted with Haas and Luther Zeigler Rosser.

At approximately 11:30 a.m., Haas insisted that Chief of Detectives Newport Alonzo Lanford arrange a search of Frank's residence, with Frank accompanying the officers.

Black testified that Haas identified himself as Frank's attorney and insisted that investigators leave nothing undone to clear his client.

The demand appeared cooperative, but prosecutors questioned its purpose.

The search occurred two days after Mary Phagan's murder. Frank had therefore had time in which incriminating material could have been removed, washed, or discarded. A search finding nothing suspicious would strengthen the appearance of his cooperation.

The prosecution argued that the next step was to direct investigators toward Lee's residence, where the bloodstained shirt was discovered.

Dorsey explicitly declared:

"Our contention is that this shirt was a plant."

He argued that the search of Frank's home was part of a plan to redirect police suspicion toward Lee.

The allegation did not establish that Haas knew the shirt had been planted or that Frank personally placed it in the barrel, but the timing and order of the searches were central to the prosecution's theory (AJ, July 31).

Haas Attempts to Control the Pinkerton Reports

The May 9 Atlanta Journal reported another incident involving Haas.

Pinkerton investigator Harry Scott testified that Frank hired the agency on behalf of the National Pencil Company on Monday, April 28, supposedly to identify Mary Phagan's murderer.

According to Scott, Haas later asked him and Pinkerton superintendent Pierce to withhold their investigative findings from police until Haas had reviewed them.

Scott and Pierce refused, maintaining that they would rather withdraw from the investigation than accept the restriction.

The contrast was striking. Haas insisted that police search Frank's home while separately seeking to examine the private detectives' findings before those findings reached investigators.

An attorney may seek information for a client's defense, but attempting to control the reporting of evidence raised legitimate questions about the independence of an investigation conducted while the attorney's client was under suspicion (AJ, May 9, 6).

Third Piece of Evidence: The Murder Notes

Two handwritten notes were discovered near Mary Phagan's body early Sunday morning, April 27.

The messages contained unusual spelling and grammar and referred to a Black man and the night watchman.

Their wording threatened to direct suspicion toward Lee.

On April 29, The Atlanta Journal reported that three handwriting examiners believed Lee had written the notes.

Their opinions initially strengthened suspicion against him, although the comparisons did not conclusively establish authorship (AJ, April 29, 1).

James Conley Admits Writing the Notes

The investigation changed when National Pencil Company sweeper James Conley admitted writing the notes.

Conley initially gave conflicting accounts of their origin. By late May, he accused Frank of instructing him to prepare them.

During Frank's trial on Monday, August 4, Conley testified that Frank had supplied the writing materials and dictated the messages.

Frank denied the accusation, and the defense challenged Conley's credibility.

Conley's admission established that the notes were fabricated. Whether Frank directed their creation remained disputed.

If Conley's accusation was truthful, the notes were part of an effort to create false evidence that could implicate the night watchman (AJ, August 4).

Frank Confronts Lee at Police Headquarters

One of the most revealing portions of the May 9 Journal concerned a private conversation between Frank and Lee.

Detectives Harry Scott and John R. Black asked Frank to speak with Lee because they suspected the watchman knew more about the murder than he had disclosed.

Lee was handcuffed to a chair when Frank entered.

According to Lee, he complained about being detained for a crime he had not committed.

Frank replied that he believed Lee was innocent but thought he possessed information about the murder. The defense would keep this narrative going throughout the entire trial to create doubt.

Lee attempted to explain that he had patrolled the second floor every half hour and would have noticed something unusual if the killing occurred there during his rounds.

According to Lee, Frank interrupted and scolded him:

"Let's don't talk about that. Let that go."

The exchange raised questions about Frank's intentions. 

The interview was supposedly intended to obtain information, yet Frank allegedly discouraged Lee from explaining his movements.

Scott testified that Lee afterward complained that Frank had not genuinely attempted to obtain the truth.

Frank disputed the implication that he had tried to silence the watchman (AJ, May 9, 6).

The Coroner's Jury Holds Both Men

The coroner's jury concluded its investigation at approximately 6:30 p.m. Thursday, May 8.

The jurors determined that Mary Phagan died from strangulation and recommended holding both Frank and Lee for investigation by the Fulton County grand jury.

Deputy Sheriff Plennie Minor delivered the news at the Fulton County jail.

Frank was reading a newspaper and indicated that he expected the decision. He showed no emotions. It was an odd thing for a supposedly innocent man to act that way.

Lee appeared depressed and lowered his head dejectedly.

Neither Scott nor Black claimed to possess conclusive evidence identifying the murderer when the inquest ended (AJ, 6).

The Prosecution's Theory: Manufacturing a Murderer

The prosecution later argued that the three pieces of evidence were intended to work together.

The time slip would suggest that Lee had abandoned his duties.

The blood-soaked shirt would appear to explain the missing time as a trip home to change clothing.

The murder notes would direct suspicion toward a Black man associated with the factory's night watch.

Frank's changing interpretation of the clock record was central to that argument.

On Sunday, he reportedly declared the punches satisfactory. On Monday, he identified discrepancies.

Detective Black later testified that Frank suggested those gaps gave Lee time to travel home and return, and that the remarks influenced the search of Lee's residence.

The bloody shirt found there appeared to have been stained while unworn. Conley later admitted writing the murder notes and accused Frank of dictating them.

During the August closing arguments, Assistant Solicitor General Frank Arthur Hooper accused Frank of attempting to sacrifice the watchman to protect himself.

The allegation rested upon circumstantial evidence and disputed testimony. No eyewitness established that Frank personally altered the time slip or planted the shirt (AC, August 22, 2).

Conclusion: The Attempt to Frame Newt Lee

The May 9, 1913, Atlanta Journal documents how Newt Lee, the night watchman who reported Mary Phagan's murder, became a suspect under circumstances that deserved serious scrutiny.

Lee described Frank's unusual instructions, his handling of the time clock nervously (a foreshadowing?), and their private confrontation at police headquarters.

The subsequent investigation exposed a troubling pattern.

Sunday to Monday to Tuesday

Frank reportedly described Lee's time slip as satisfactory on Sunday, then identified missing punches on Monday. Detective Black later testified that Frank suggested those gaps gave Lee enough time to go home and return, after which police searched Lee's residence.

The bloodstained shirt discovered there on Tuesday appeared to have been stained while unworn. 

Conley subsequently admitted writing the murder notes and accused Frank of dictating them. Conley stated the purpose of the notes was to frame Newt Lee. 

Herbert Haas's involvement raised additional questions. He demanded that police search Frank's home while separately seeking to "review" Pinkerton findings before they reached investigators.

The prosecution argued that these circumstances revealed an attempt to manufacture evidence against Lee. It was a logical inference. 

The defense disputed that interpretation, and the surviving record does not conclusively establish Frank's personal responsibility for altering the time slip or planting the shirt.

Nevertheless, the contradictions in the time-clock testimony, the suspicious condition of the shirt, the fabricated murder notes, and the conduct of Frank's defense team formed the basis of the prosecution's argument that Frank attempted to make Newt Lee responsible for Mary Phagan's murder.
