The End of the Vance Heir Apparent: Midterm Bloodbath, the Iran War, and the Unraveling of MAGA Succession

Maga is dead! Put a fork in it Trump killed it... 

Reports circulating through CNN and allied channels paint Vice President JD Vance as demoralized and actively reconsidering a 2028 presidential bid in the wake of what the video frames as a blue tsunami midterm. The numbers, as summarized from those sources, show Republican losses across the House, the Senate, and state-level contests that exceeded typical midterm swings by roughly double the historical average. Allies speaking to reporters describe Vance wrestling with ambition against the practical realities of a fractured coalition, the demands of a fourth child born this summer, and the simple arithmetic of age. At forty-two he remains young enough for a later cycle, yet the immediate environment makes a run now appear unviable to those closest to him.

The Iran war sits at the center of the difficulty. Multiple voices in the reporting state that if the conflict continues, no Republican candidate can win the general election in 2028. Vance has reportedly placed primary blame for the midterm results on the war itself. That framing drew a sharp public rebuke from Senator John Kennedy of Louisiana, who told him, in substance, to put down the crackpipe. Kennedy’s point, delivered on live television, was that voters such as the hypothetical Toby and Edith shifted because of persistent economic pain: wages rising only 1.3 percent against inflation running near 4 percent. The video notes that inflation was lower when Biden left office than it stands under the current administration, and that corruption and tariff effects also registered with the electorate. Reducing the outcome to a single foreign-policy variable therefore understates the broader failure to deliver on affordability and restraint.

Historical precedent reinforces the structural problem. Vice presidents almost never succeed their presidents at the ballot box. George H. W. Bush remains the clear modern exception; Al Gore and Kamala Harris stand as more recent illustrations of the rule. Trump has not committed to an endorsement and has indicated he prefers the primary process to play out. His own unpopularity, measured in multiple polls, further complicates any successor’s path. At the same time, the MAGA base itself shows signs of fracture. Pollster Rich Baris is cited describing a sense of betrayal among 2024 Trump supporters, particularly men, younger voters, Latinos, and white non-college-educated voters, over unfulfilled promises on cost of living and the absence of new wars. Rebuilding that coalition would require Vance to construct a new populist formation rather than simply inherit the old one. Allies believe he would dominate a primary if he entered, given financial ties to figures such as Peter Thiel and residual organizational strength, yet dominance in a primary does not automatically translate into a general-election majority when the president’s numbers remain underwater and the war continues.

Potential competitors already visible include Ron DeSantis, Ted Cruz, and Brian Kemp. Tucker Carlson has been noted as possibly teasing a third-party option, which would further split the right. Stephen Miller, now White House Chief of Staff, is positioned in the reporting as central to any effort to re-energize the base. The practical question is whether Miller’s focus on policy and messaging can offset the cumulative weight of economic results, ongoing military commitments, and the perception that the administration has not delivered the restraint and prosperity voters expected.

The punishments under SB 1134 are:
Officials commit misfeasance or malfeasance in office
Any county commissioner, city council member, or other local official acting in their official capacity who violates the law (e.g., by having the city organize, fund, or promote a prohibited event) commits misfeasance or malfeasance in office. In Florida, this can result in suspension or removal from office by the Governor. 

Residents can sue the city or county
A resident can bring a lawsuit in circuit court against the local government. The court can award: Declaratory relief (a ruling that the city violated the law)
Injunctive relief (an order stopping the violation)
Damages
Costs

The internship offered a $1,000 stipend, part-time in-person work during the 2027 legislative session (roughly early January–mid-May) in the offices of Sen. Jodeh and Rep. Yara Zokaie at the Colorado Capitol.
Other requirements included being a current undergraduate with a minimum 3.5 GPA, interest in policy/social change/justice/the legislative process, and flexibility.
Applications went to a Colorado General Assembly email (iman.jodeh.aide@coleg.gov), with a November 30, 2026 deadline.
Jodeh and Zokaie co-founded the caucus in 2024 to advocate for MENASA and Muslim communities and to combat xenophobia and Islamophobia. Jodeh has posted similar identity-restricted internship notices before (e.g., a 2023 “Arab or Muslim” internship).⁠Thegatewaypundit
The posts were deleted from her Instagram (and reportedly Facebook) after criticism, including from accounts like Libs of TikTok that highlighted the criteria and tagged the Department of Justice’s Civil Rights Division.⁠Newsbusters

Legal context
The position is a paid internship in a public legislative office. Title VII of the Civil Rights Act and Colorado’s Anti-Discrimination Act generally prohibit employment discrimination based on religion or national origin/ancestry. Commentators and some reports note that an explicit identity requirement of this kind for a paid public role raises clear legal concerns, though no formal complaint, EEOC action, or DOJ enforcement has been reported in coverage to date. A DOJ spokesperson told Newsweek they are committed to enforcing civil rights laws evenly and would look at the specific posting.⁠Newsweek

text:
One of the group struggled at first with the classic human reflex: the need to manage, to stay in control, to analyze instead of surrender. We stayed close, offering only the lightest verbal anchors. Each time he edged closer to release, the medicine met him with patience rather than force. Slowly the grip loosened. Eventually he dropped fully, and the relief that followed was almost audible in the room.
Another carried a long habit of emotional control. The medicine did not negotiate. It met him face-to-face, and the confrontation was honest. He purged—clean, purposeful, necessary—and on the other side of that release found a state of pure experiencing that required no commentary, no defense, no story. Just presence.
Throughout both the morning and afternoon sessions, the lasers remained available as an optional doorway into the particular visual phenomena Goler and others have described—the recurring geometric structures and code-like symbols that appear within the diffracted light. Some chose to engage that exploration; others remained fully immersed in the inner landscapes the medicine itself presented. Either way, the container stayed the same: careful, non-directive, and devoted entirely to personal discovery.
What became clear, again, is that deep medicine is not always about receiving concise answers, tidy information, or clear instruction from the other side. Sometimes the molecule seems to laugh at our direct questions. It refuses to hand over a neat download and instead points us back toward the slower, more ordinary work of connecting—with ourselves, with one another, with the texture of daily life—and discovering the answers that can only be found by living them. The real gift is often the capacity it restores: the ability to listen inward, to trust what arises in the quiet of terrestrial experience, and to keep doing the work long after the session ends.
In the end, the depth of any such journey remains profoundly subjective. No one standing outside it can measure its value or declare its meaning. Only the one who walked it can know what it offered, what it asked, and what it ultimately revealed.
The room itself seemed to breathe with them. Connection moved in every direction: connection to self, yes, but also to the people sharing the space, to the quiet clink of a water glass later, to the cultural threads each person carried, to the shifting perceptions that make ordinary reality feel newly transparent. Psychedelic medicines have a way of dissolving the usual filters so that understanding can arrive not as theory but as direct knowing. In scientific language we might speak of temporary shifts in default-mode network activity, increased neural entropy, or enhanced binding of serotonin receptors. In the language of the experience itself, it simply feels like the universe deciding to show you a few more of its cards—and then sitting with you while you decide what to do with them.
We were not offering therapy that day. We were offering a carefully held container for people who already knew how to meet themselves. The medicine did the rest. And when the final session softened and the gongs spoke one last time, the seven of us remained for a while in the quiet afterglow—feet still pointed toward the center, hearts a little more open than when we had begun.

text:
Metropolis doesn't walk; it stampedes. Elevated trains thunder above canyons of buff limestone and polished chrome, newsboys shout afternoon extras through exhaust haze, and forty stories overhead, a colossal gilded globe turns lazily atop the Daily Planet building like a second sun tethered to Ninth Street.

Up in the twelfth-floor city room, seventy Underwood typewriters hammer out a steady iron rain. Perry White stalks between desks chomping an unlit Panatela cigar down to wet shreds, bellowing for shipping manifests while teenaged copyboy Jimmy Olsen—all freckles, red cowlick, and crooked green bow tie—dodges flying wastebaskets with wet darkroom prints clipped to his sleeve.

Clark Kent fits into the corner desk near the water cooler almost too well. He hunches two inches out of his true height, speaks half an octave softer than necessary, fumbles revolving doors, and lets sharper reporters raid his pencil cup. Lois Lane, seated six feet away in a razor-cut navy pinstripe suit with a tilted felt hat pinned over dark curls, sizes up Perry's new hire in roughly four seconds and writes him off as harmless Kansas wallpaper.

She has bigger game tonight. Two stories, actually, neither of which Perry wants touching libel court without hard proof: at midnight, Evelyn Curry goes to the electric chair at State Penitentiary for a fatal shooting Lois suspects was committed by brassy nightclub singer Claire, and downtown, sleek munitions lobbyist Alex Greer is quietly bribing Senator Barrows to push through an emergency defense contract tied to black-market exotic weaponry.

"Stick to flower shows, Kent," Lois tosses over her shoulder, snatching her handbag as the five-o'clock whistle blows. "Real news bites."

Clark smiles mildly, adjusts his horn-rimmed glasses, waits until the elevator doors slide shut, and steps calmly out the open twelfth-story washroom window into rushing twilight air.

Earth's yellow sun has soaked into him for twenty-four years now; he doesn't merely leap, as he did in Smallville's pastures—he rides Earth's magnetic lines like a hawk on a thermal, crimson cape snapping clean above harbor tugboats.

By ten-thirty, guided by telescanner vision piercing coastal fog, he intercepts Claire packing steamer trunks aboard a Panama-bound freighter at Pier 9. One look at a six-foot-three stranger in primary colors hovering serenely outside her locked brass porthole drains every drop of bravado from her painted lips; within ten minutes she scribbles a seven-page confession naming her accomplices.

At 11:57 PM, cold rain needles the slate roof of the Governor's Mansion.

Down in the foyer, two state troopers whirl as boots thud softly onto the front veranda. When the tall figure in blue and red ignores their barked warning and grasps the two-inch solid steel security door with bare hands, both troopers open fire with Thompson submachine guns.

Lead slugs flatten like dropped nickels against the crimson S across his chest, tinkling harmlessly onto the parquet floor.

He doesn't strike the troopers. He gently plucks both hot barrels from their hands, knots the steel gun-tubes together like wet licorice, peels the reinforced vault door off its hinges to climb the grand staircase, and deposits a bound, spitting Claire—alongside her signed confession—squarely atop the Governor's quilted bedspread with ninety seconds left before the prison dynamo throws its switch. Leaning against the mahogany bedpost with arms folded, he waits politely until the trembling Governor screams Evelyn Curry's stay of execution into the candlestick telephone, then offers a quiet goodnight and blurs out the open French doors.

Crossing the Lower East Side tenements on his way home, his hearing—tuned too wide, perhaps, in the exhilaration of open sky—catches a woman's sharp cry and the ugly snap of cowhide behind a fourth-floor curtain. Glass shatters inward as he lands between a terrified seamstress and her drunken husband. The brute lunges with a pearl-handled switchblade; steel meets bare collarbone and snaps clean in half. One open-handed shove sends the man through a lath-and-plaster partition into his own icebox—alive, unbroken, and permanently cured of lifting a belt—while the stranger pauses only long enough to drape a fallen wool shawl over the wife's shaking shoulders before leaping back into the mist.

By noon the next day, Metropolis talks of nothing else. A circus acrobat? A Martian? A secret New Deal project?

Lois Lane is furious she missed him, which is probably why she lets mild-mannered Clark talk her into dinner at the Chez Pierre supper club that evening—mostly because she knows lobbyist Alex Greer drinks champagne in the back VIP alcove, and Clark makes a convenient decoy. Halfway through the soup course, Greer's chief enforcer, a thick-necked bruiser named Butch Matson who dislikes reporters eyeing his boss's booth, swagger-steps up to their table, blows cigar smoke in Clark's face, and grabs Lois's wrist for a rumba.

Clark puts on a masterclass in cowardice. He stammers, knocks over a breadbasket, apologizes to Matson's cufflinks, and edges backward toward the coatroom while crimson fury rises up Lois's throat.

Lois slaps Matson clean across the jaw herself, flings her linen napkin into Clark's minestrone, and marches out into the rain, swearing she wouldn't cross a puddle on Clark Kent's coat.

She makes it half a block before tires screech against wet cobblestones. An emerald-green sedan jumps the curb; Matson and three gunmen yank Lois off her heels into the backseat, roaring north onto the winding cliffside asphalt of the Palisades Road to dump nosy Miss Lane into the Hudson.

Two miles past the city limits, Matson's high beams slice the fog—and illuminate two scarlet boots planted wide on the double yellow line.

"Run him flat!" Matson barks.

The driver floors it. Eighty miles an hour. Seventy yards. Twenty.

Hands close beneath the chrome front bumper. Metal shrieks like a slaughtered hog as two tons of Detroit steel stop dead, rear wheels spinning wildly in empty air. Inside the cab, Matson's pistol clatters across the dashboard while Lois presses both palms against the cracked safety glass, scarcely breathing. Effortlessly—almost thoughtfully, as though checking the weight of a melon—the caped man lifts the emerald-green sedan clear above his head, tilts it forty degrees until Matson and his three trigger-men spill howling onto the roadside weeds, and brings the empty automobile smashing nose-first down against a granite boulder in a shower of sparks and radiator steam.

Before Matson's crew can scramble past the ditch, strong arms scoop Lois out of the damp grass. For forty dizzying seconds she smells crisp high-altitude ozone and, strangely enough, clean dry hay, watching harbor lights wheel far beneath her heels before he sets her gently beside a streetcar kiosk near Printing House Square.

"Tell Mr. White," says a warm baritone she almost—though surely not—thinks she has heard before, "that Miss Curry is having breakfast at home."

Up he goes, clearing an elevated railway trestle in a single soaring arc. Two hours later, Lois rips her third sheet out of the roller, types SUPERMAN in forty-point headline caps, and hands Perry White the biggest morning edition since Lindbergh.

AN OPEN LETTER TO GEORGE W. BUSH: TWENTY-FIVE YEARS AFTER 9/11, EXPLAIN “ISLAM IS A RELIGION OF PEACE”

THE EVIDENCE™

The evidence will be presented. The verdict is yours.

Dear President Bush:

Your administration repeatedly advanced the declaration that “Islam is a religion of peace.” Your press secretary, Ari Fleischer, explicitly identified it as your position. Twenty-five years after September 11, Americans are entitled to ask what justified that sweeping assurance and how you reconcile it with the continuing violence of organizations invoking Islamic authority.

The wording and chronology deserve precision. At the Islamic Center of Washington on September 17, 2001, your exact words were “Islam is peace.” The longer formulation became an expressly stated administration position. This letter addresses that broader declaration, rather than attributing the longer sentence to your September 17 speech.

You were speaking to a wounded country. Americans had watched people leap from burning buildings. Families were searching for loved ones. The nation needed leadership, an accurate explanation of the enemy, and assurance that the government would protect its citizens.

Your mosque visit addressed another immediate concern. You described Muslim women afraid to leave their homes and reminded Americans that their Muslim neighbors included military personnel, physicians, business owners, and parents. You condemned intimidation against innocent people. That was a legitimate exercise of presidential leadership.

But protecting those citizens did not require you to pronounce a definitive judgment on the nature of Islam. You could have defended their rights, condemned retaliation, and insisted on individual accountability without presenting a sweeping religious conclusion as an established fact.

What qualified your administration to settle which interpretation of Islam was authentic?

YOUR DECLARATION LEFT THE CENTRAL QUESTION UNANSWERED

The terrorists claimed religious justification. You rejected their claim. That rejection expressed a moral judgment, but it did not explain how their interpretation developed, why it attracted followers, or how its influence could be defeated.

Those questions were essential. An ideology does not lose its influence because a president declares that its adherents misunderstand their religion. Its arguments must be examined, its recruitment understood, its organizations disrupted, and its claims challenged.

A useful explanation would have distinguished ordinary Muslim religious practice from Islamist political movements and violent jihadist organizations. Those categories involve different beliefs, conduct, and objectives. The declaration that Islam is a religion of peace offered Americans little help in understanding those distinctions.

YOUR ADMINISTRATION WAS ASKED TO EXPLAIN

This concern was raised while you were president. At an October 16, 2002, press briefing, a reporter challenged the administration’s characterization of Islam, citing passages of the Quran. Fleischer rejected the question’s premise and reaffirmed your position. He then argued against blaming innocent people or an entire religion for terrorists’ actions.

His defense of innocent people addressed collective blame. It did not resolve the underlying question about religious interpretation. Whether a particular passage supports the reporter’s reading requires examination of the text and its context. Reaffirming a presidential belief cannot perform that work.

That distinction remains significant. Defending a citizen against an unsupported accusation and evaluating a religious doctrine are different responsibilities. Your administration repeatedly answered questions about the second by emphasizing the first.

TWENTY-FIVE YEARS LATER, THE THREAT REMAINS

The Institute for Economics & Peace’s Global Terrorism Index 2026 identifies Islamic State, Jamaat Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin, Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan, and al-Shabaab as the four deadliest terrorist organizations in 2025. Militant Islamist organizations remain central to the international terrorist threat a quarter-century after September 11.

The institute describes Islamic State’s dispersed affiliate network, JNIM’s expansion in the Sahel, the Pakistani Taliban’s resurgence, and al-Shabaab’s persistence despite military pressure. These organizations exploit instability and adapt to changing conditions. Their survival requires an explanation that examines both their ideology and the circumstances enabling their operations.

Their continuing violence does not establish that peaceful interpretations of Islam are insincere or nonexistent. It does establish that a general assurance about peace is insufficient to explain the movements committing that violence.

How did your declaration help Americans understand the religious arguments these organizations use to recruit followers and justify coercion?

THE EVIDENCE REQUIRES HONESTY IN BOTH DIRECTIONS

There is also evidence of improvement. The 2026 index reports that worldwide terrorism deaths declined by 28 percent in 2025. That is significant. An honest assessment must acknowledge progress alongside the persistence of dangerous organizations.

The existence of Islamist terrorism cannot establish the guilt of an individual Muslim. An accusation against a person requires evidence about that person. Religious affiliation alone cannot supply it. Your insistence that innocent Americans should be protected remains defensible.

But the existence of peaceful Muslims does not answer every criticism of Islamic teachings, religious institutions, or movements seeking political power. Personal innocence and institutional scrutiny are separate questions. Neither cancels the other.

Americans should be able to examine religious arguments for violence, restrictions on freedom of conscience, and demands for religious supremacy. Such inquiries require accurate sourcing and careful distinctions. They should receive substantive answers.

Religious freedom includes the freedom to question religion.

WHAT AMERICANS NEEDED TO HEAR

Mr. President, you could have affirmed that Muslim Americans possessed the same rights as everyone else while acknowledging that the attackers belonged to a movement whose religious arguments required serious examination.

You could have explained that the government would assess organizations through evidence about their teachings, financing, affiliations, and conduct. Public professions of peace would be considered alongside what those organizations actually supported.

You could have emphasized that peaceful worship would be protected and that recruitment for violence, threats, and assistance to terrorist organizations would receive scrutiny regardless of the religious language used to justify them.

That approach would have supplied an understandable standard: protect individual rights, investigate specific wrongdoing, and examine the ideology used to excuse it.

The phrase “Islam is a religion of peace” could reassure listeners. By itself, it could not answer their most consequential questions.

THE QUESTIONS STILL BEFORE YOU

Were you describing how peaceful Muslims understood their faith? Were you making a diplomatic statement intended to preserve cooperation? Were you offering a theological judgment? Were you attempting all three?

Those purposes are different. Each requires its own explanation.

Your September 17 speech clearly expressed concern about intimidation. It did not establish that your broad religious conclusion adequately accounted for competing interpretations or the movements acting upon them. Americans can recognize the value of your immediate purpose while challenging the reach of your words.

The record presented here also does not establish that you knowingly lied. That accusation would require evidence of your knowledge and intent. The criticism supported here is more precise: your administration offered a categorical religious assurance that did not adequately explain the enemy’s beliefs and methods.

THE FINDINGS

Your defense of innocent Muslim Americans was justified. Your administration’s declaration that Islam is a religion of peace went beyond defending their rights and provided an insufficient explanation of the ideological threat confronting the country.

Twenty-five years later, lethal Islamist organizations continue to operate. Their persistence requires scrutiny of the doctrines, institutions, networks, and conditions sustaining them. The documented decline in worldwide terrorism deaths also deserves acknowledgment.

Americans deserved leaders capable of defending religious liberty while examining religious claims used to authorize violence. Those responsibilities could—and should—have been fulfilled together.

Mr. President, you offered a memorable assurance. Twenty-five years later, Americans still deserve the explanation.

Respectfully,

Kim Wojcinski

The evidence has been presented. The verdict is yours.

COAS DEEPENS ARMY TRANSFORMATION, COMMISSIONS 120 HOMES, PRIORITISES TROOPS’ WELFARE BEYOND SERVICE

Lieutenant General Waidi Shaibu, the Chief of Army Staff, has reaffirmed the Nigerian Army’s commitment to sustained infrastructural development and improved personnel welfare. This commitment was expressed during the commissioning of 120 newly completed three-bedroom housing units on Friday 13 November 2026 at Idu, Abuja. These units are part of Phase 2 of the Affordable Home Ownership Option for All Soldiers (AHOOAS) and bring the total number of housing units delivered nationwide to 700. This further strengthens efforts to provide soldiers with decent and affordable homes after meritorious service.

COAS emphasized that the Nigerian Army’s ongoing infrastructural development encompasses modern barracks accommodation, healthcare facilities and post-service housing schemes designed to improve troops’ living conditions, boost morale and enhance operational effectiveness. He noted that the Army's transformation agenda places equal premium on combat readiness and personnel welfare, in line with his Soldier-First Culture. He further disclosed that 5 per cent of the housing units have been reserved for personnel wounded in action, reaffirming the Army’s commitment to those who have made enormous sacrifices in defence of the nation.

The COAS noted that the AHOOAS programme has progressively delivered 400 housing units in Abuja in December 2024, 60 in Ibadan in December 2025, 80 in Jos in June 2026 and 40 in Benin City on 6 November 2026, in addition to the newly commissioned 120 units. He commended the Post-Service Housing Development Limited (PHDL), project partners and successive Army leaderships, particularly the late Lieutenant General Taoreed Lagbaja and the current Chief of Defence Staff, General Olufemi Oluyede, for their contributions to the initiative.

Earlier, the Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer of PHDL, Major General Kevin Ukandu, disclosed that Phase 3 of the Idu housing project is already under construction and scheduled for completion in the first quarter of 2027. He added that the estate features a 2.5-kilometre asphalted road with drainage, a 500KVA transformer, solar-powered streetlights and a water reticulation system, reaffirming PHDL’s commitment to ensuring that more soldiers become homeowners before retirement.

*PMIF26 Concludes with Major Investment Agreements, Pakistan Reaffirms Commitment to Mineral Value Addition*

_The 2-day forum brought together over 10,000 attendees, 122 exhibitors and participation from more than 60 countries_ 

*ISLAMABAD, November 13, 2026:* The two-day Pakistan Minerals Investment Forum 2026 (PMIF26) concluded in Islamabad on Friday with Prime Minister Muhammad Shehbaz Sharif inviting international investors to explore Pakistan’s mineral wealth, assuring them of investment protection and government support, while calling for a shift from exporting raw minerals to developing domestic processing and refining facilities.
Addressing the concluding day of the forum, attended by over 10,000 participants from more than 60 countries, the prime minister declared, “Your safety is our safety,” and pledged to address concerns and facilitate investment in the mining and minerals sector. He stressed that Pakistan must move beyond exporting unprocessed resources and establish facilities to convert raw materials into finished and semi-finished products, generating greater economic value, employment, technical expertise and technology transfer. Referring to a Goldman Sachs projection that Pakistan could become the world’s sixth-largest economy by 2075, PM Shehbaz said he hoped the country would achieve the milestone earlier than 2050.

The prime minister, accompanied by Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir, also inaugurated the National Minerals Data Centre and the Geological Survey of Pakistan (GSP) GeoPortal. The digital platforms are designed to improve access to geological information, support mineral exploration, reduce uncertainty for investors and facilitate informed investment decisions.

In his address, Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir said Pakistan’s ambition extended beyond exporting raw minerals to developing the complete value chain domestically, including refining and manufacturing. He described turning the country’s mineral wealth into tangible economic gains as a collective national goal and stressed that communities in mineral-rich areas must benefit directly from mining projects. He called for long-term partnerships that generate lasting value for Pakistan and its partners, urging the country to move “from potential to production, from promises to action, and from raw exports to value-added growth”.

A major announcement during the forum came from the Frontier Works Organization (FWO), which announced an estimated 350 million tonnes of copper in the Dasht-e-Kain area of Chagai, Balochistan, based on approximately half of its drilling data analysed so far. The announcement highlighted the exploration potential of Pakistan and added to the range of investment opportunities presented during the forum. 

Mari Minerals announced the discovery of its first-ever gold and copper reserves in Chagai. The reserve has a potential of around 1 billion tonnes of copper and gold. The National Resources Limited (NRL) announced a $100 million investment in Pakistan’s mineral sector.

Federal Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik outlined Pakistan's push into critical minerals like copper, gold, lithium, and antimony, emphasizing domestic refining, advanced geological mapping, and infrastructure upgrades like the Rohri-Nokundi railway to link mineral hubs globally.

OGDC President Ahmed Hayat Lak celebrated PMIF26's success in forging international partnerships and launching digital data portals, stressing that execution, technical excellence, and transparent policies are vital to turning mineral wealth into lasting economic progress.

Diverse conference sessions covered AI exploration, infrastructure security, and environmental standards, complemented by an international exhibition where participants signed 13 major agreements and MoUs before concluding with an invitation to the next forum in November 2027.

Everyone is watching one man step down, and allegations still unproven in court. A friend in the industry told me something else. This is his account. I have not verified it. It is not established fact.

He said that 128 GB300 units, recently out of Hsinchu, are being offered for rent in Shenzhen — on five-year contracts. Five years, he added, is normal now.

A few months ago, he was taken to sit in on a Shenzhen group that flips Nvidia GPUs and overseas data centers. People in that role, he said, are not rare. I will not name anyone. The system is still running.

His read is that Nvidia needs cash from GPUs that actually get sold, he said, because many of the GPUs are being financed by the supply chain. If that is right, Taiwan's vendors carry the cash and the compliance risk: the rental desk is in Shenzhen, and the financing sits here.

These people, he said, now stay ahead of U.S. tracking. Over the past year they have been buying Japanese data-center companies that can pass U.S. review. Washington chases where the chips go. They buy compute that can clear review.

The gray market is not a secret. International reports this year already had high-end AI servers trading at multiples of list price on the mainland, often via Hong Kong and Shenzhen, and Washington is debating rules on remote access to overseas data centers. My friend was more specific: the new route, he said, runs through Japan.

Two questions.

Chips iterate this fast, and you sign a five-year contract — what do you do with the hardware in year five, barbecue on it?

News Grind

Arabica coffee futures traded around $3.1 per pound, a level not seen since March, as traders weighed signs of tightening inventories while monitoring the pace of Brazil's harvest. Arabica certified stocks at ICE fell by another 3,069 bags to 377,465, the lowest level since March 2024. The market also factored in delays to Brazil’s harvest due to rainfall in major producing areas, alongside quality concerns, with investment funds increasing activity amid weather uncertainties. Coffee harvest in Brazil reached 44% as of June 24, below 51% a year earlier and the five-year average of 47%, according to Safras & Mercado. Brazilian coffee, beef and tropical fruit will still be tariffed 40%, says Brazil’s vice president

RIO DE JANEIRO — Brazilian Vice President Geraldo Alckmin said Saturday that Brazilian exported goods to the U.S. including coffee, beef and tropical fruits would still be tariffed 40%, despite President Donald Trump’s decision to remove some import taxes.

In a dramatic move on Friday, Trump scrapped levies announced in April on what he called ‘Liberation Day’ in hopes of encouraging domestic production and lifting the U.S. economy. Brazil at the time was hit with a 10% tariff.

But in July, Trump imposed a further 40% tariff, citing — among other reasons — the trial of his ally, former President Jair Bolsonaro, which he called a “witch hunt.” Proceedings went ahead regardless and in September Bolsonaro was sentenced to 27 years and three months in prison for attempting a coup.

Alckmin said some products, such as orange juice, would now have a zero tariff as they were not targeted by the additional 40%. But that extra tariff remains in place on products including coffee, beef and tropical fruits, such as mangos and pineapples.

While Brazil’s vice president welcomed Trump’s latest decision, which he called “positive” and a “step in the right direction,” he said there remained a “distortion that needs to be corrected.”

“Everyone got 10% less, but in Brazil’s case, which had 50%, we ended up with 40%, which is very high,” Alckmin told journalists in the capital Brasilia.

Alckmin said that Friday's decision means that 26% of Brazilian goods are now entering the U.S. without additional tariffs. That's up from 23%.

Trump’s July decision, which was overtly political as Brazil has a trade deficit with the United States, led to the worst U.S.-Brazil relations in history.

Those relations have since improved, and in October Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Trump met in Malaysia.

“President Lula’s conversation with President Donald Trump was important in terms of dialogue and negotiation,” Alckmin said on Saturday.

After that encounter, Lula said he was confident the two countries would soon reach a trade deal.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Brazil’s Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira met for 50 minutes this week to further the conversation.

The Trump administration has insisted that its tariffs helped fill government coffers and weren’t a major factor in higher prices at grocery stores around the country. But Democrats were quick to paint Friday’s move as an acknowledgment that Trump’s policies were hurting American pocketbooks.

Record-high beef prices have been a particular concern, and Trump had said he intended to take action to try and lower them. Trump’s tariffs on Brazil, a major beef exporter, had been a factor.

Back in Brazil, the Brazilian Association of the Coffee Industry said it would continue to monitor the situation.

“(We) will keep working to ensure legal certainty, competitiveness, and predictability for the Brazilian coffee industry,” the group’s president, Pavel Cardoso, said in a statement. (Wires, A.I News)

Brazilian coffee, beef and tropical fruit will still be tariffed 40%, says Brazil’s vice president

RIO DE JANEIRO — Brazilian Vice President Geraldo Alckmin said Saturday that Brazilian exported goods to the U.S. including coffee, beef and tropical fruits would still be tariffed 40%, despite President Donald Trump’s decision to remove some import taxes.

In a dramatic move on Friday, Trump scrapped levies announced in April on what he called ‘Liberation Day’ in hopes of encouraging domestic production and lifting the U.S. economy. Brazil at the time was hit with a 10% tariff.

But in July, Trump imposed a further 40% tariff, citing — among other reasons — the trial of his ally, former President Jair Bolsonaro, which he called a “witch hunt.” Proceedings went ahead regardless and in September Bolsonaro was sentenced to 27 years and three months in prison for attempting a coup.

Alckmin said some products, such as orange juice, would now have a zero tariff as they were not targeted by the additional 40%. But that extra tariff remains in place on products including coffee, beef and tropical fruits, such as mangos and pineapples.

While Brazil’s vice president welcomed Trump’s latest decision, which he called “positive” and a “step in the right direction,” he said there remained a “distortion that needs to be corrected.”

“Everyone got 10% less, but in Brazil’s case, which had 50%, we ended up with 40%, which is very high,” Alckmin told journalists in the capital Brasilia.

Alckmin said that Friday's decision means that 26% of Brazilian goods are now entering the U.S. without additional tariffs. That's up from 23%.

Trump’s July decision, which was overtly political as Brazil has a trade deficit with the United States, led to the worst U.S.-Brazil relations in history.

Those relations have since improved, and in October Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Trump met in Malaysia.

“President Lula’s conversation with President Donald Trump was important in terms of dialogue and negotiation,” Alckmin said on Saturday.

After that encounter, Lula said he was confident the two countries would soon reach a trade deal.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Brazil’s Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira met for 50 minutes this week to further the conversation.

The Trump administration has insisted that its tariffs helped fill government coffers and weren’t a major factor in higher prices at grocery stores around the country. But Democrats were quick to paint Friday’s move as an acknowledgment that Trump’s policies were hurting American pocketbooks.

Record-high beef prices have been a particular concern, and Trump had said he intended to take action to try and lower them. Trump’s tariffs on Brazil, a major beef exporter, had been a factor.

Back in Brazil, the Brazilian Association of the Coffee Industry said it would continue to monitor the situation.

“(We) will keep working to ensure legal certainty, competitiveness, and predictability for the Brazilian coffee industry,” the group’s president, Pavel Cardoso, said in a statement. (Wires, A.I News)

Brazilian coffee, beef and tropical fruit will still be tariffed 40%, says Brazil’s vice president

RIO DE JANEIRO — Brazilian Vice President Geraldo Alckmin said Saturday that Brazilian exported goods to the U.S. including coffee, beef and tropical fruits would still be tariffed 40%, despite President Donald Trump’s decision to remove some import taxes.

In a dramatic move on Friday, Trump scrapped levies announced in April on what he called ‘Liberation Day’ in hopes of encouraging domestic production and lifting the U.S. economy. Brazil at the time was hit with a 10% tariff.

But in July, Trump imposed a further 40% tariff, citing — among other reasons — the trial of his ally, former President Jair Bolsonaro, which he called a “witch hunt.” Proceedings went ahead regardless and in September Bolsonaro was sentenced to 27 years and three months in prison for attempting a coup.

Alckmin said some products, such as orange juice, would now have a zero tariff as they were not targeted by the additional 40%. But that extra tariff remains in place on products including coffee, beef and tropical fruits, such as mangos and pineapples.

While Brazil’s vice president welcomed Trump’s latest decision, which he called “positive” and a “step in the right direction,” he said there remained a “distortion that needs to be corrected.”

“Everyone got 10% less, but in Brazil’s case, which had 50%, we ended up with 40%, which is very high,” Alckmin told journalists in the capital Brasilia.

Alckmin said that Friday's decision means that 26% of Brazilian goods are now entering the U.S. without additional tariffs. That's up from 23%.

Trump’s July decision, which was overtly political as Brazil has a trade deficit with the United States, led to the worst U.S.-Brazil relations in history.

Those relations have since improved, and in October Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Trump met in Malaysia.

“President Lula’s conversation with President Donald Trump was important in terms of dialogue and negotiation,” Alckmin said on Saturday.

After that encounter, Lula said he was confident the two countries would soon reach a trade deal.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Brazil’s Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira met for 50 minutes this week to further the conversation.

The Trump administration has insisted that its tariffs helped fill government coffers and weren’t a major factor in higher prices at grocery stores around the country. But Democrats were quick to paint Friday’s move as an acknowledgment that Trump’s policies were hurting American pocketbooks.

Record-high beef prices have been a particular concern, and Trump had said he intended to take action to try and lower them. Trump’s tariffs on Brazil, a major beef exporter, had been a factor.

Back in Brazil, the Brazilian Association of the Coffee Industry said it would continue to monitor the situation.

“(We) will keep working to ensure legal certainty, competitiveness, and predictability for the Brazilian coffee industry,” the group’s president, Pavel Cardoso, said in a statement. (Wires, A.I News)

PMIF26 Concludes with Major Investment Agreements, Pakistan Reaffirms Commitment to Mineral Value Addition

The 2-day forum brought together over 10,000 attendees, 122 exhibitors and participation from more than 60 countries

ISLAMABAD, November 13, 2026: The two-day Pakistan Minerals Investment Forum 2026 (PMIF26) concluded in Islamabad on Friday with Prime Minister Muhammad Shehbaz Sharif inviting international investors to explore Pakistan’s mineral wealth, assuring them of investment protection and government support, while calling for a shift from exporting raw minerals to developing domestic processing and refining facilities.
Addressing the concluding day of the forum, attended by over 10,000 participants from more than 60 countries, the prime minister declared, “Your safety is our safety,” and pledged to address concerns and facilitate investment in the mining and minerals sector. He stressed that Pakistan must move beyond exporting unprocessed resources and establish facilities to convert raw materials into finished and semi-finished products, generating greater economic value, employment, technical expertise and technology transfer. Referring to a Goldman Sachs projection that Pakistan could become the world’s sixth-largest economy by 2075, PM Shehbaz said he hoped the country would achieve the milestone earlier than 2050.

The prime minister, accompanied by Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir, also inaugurated the National Minerals Data Centre and the Geological Survey of Pakistan (GSP) GeoPortal. The digital platforms are designed to improve access to geological information, support mineral exploration, reduce uncertainty for investors and facilitate informed investment decisions.

In his address, Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir said Pakistan’s ambition extended beyond exporting raw minerals to developing the complete value chain domestically, including refining and manufacturing. He described turning the country’s mineral wealth into tangible economic gains as a collective national goal and stressed that communities in mineral-rich areas must benefit directly from mining projects. He called for long-term partnerships that generate lasting value for Pakistan and its partners, urging the country to move “from potential to production, from promises to action, and from raw exports to value-added growth”. He said Pakistan’s resources offered opportunities, while its people remained the strength needed to turn them into results.

A major announcement during the forum came from the Frontier Works Organization (FWO), which announced an estimated 350 million tonnes of copper in the Dasht-e-Kain area of Chagai, Balochistan, based on approximately half of its drilling data analysed so far. The announcement highlighted the exploration potential of Pakistan and added to the range of investment opportunities presented during the forum. 

Mari Minerals announced the discovery of its first-ever gold and copper reserves in Chagai. The reserve has a potential of around 1 billion tonnes of copper and gold. The National Resources Limited (NRL) announced a $100 million investment in Pakistan’s mineral sector.

Federal Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik outlined Pakistan's push into critical minerals like copper, gold, lithium, and antimony, emphasizing domestic refining, advanced geological mapping, and infrastructure upgrades like the Rohri-Nokundi railway to link mineral hubs globally.

OGDC President Ahmed Hayat Lak celebrated PMIF26's success in forging international partnerships and launching digital data portals, stressing that execution, technical excellence, and transparent policies are vital to turning mineral wealth into lasting economic progress.

Global mining leaders, including executives from Barrick Mining, Ivanhoe Mines, and Minmetals, shared international insights on policy certainty and regional cooperation during high-level strategic dialogues.

Here are the 5 most interesting blockchain fundraises for the week ending 11/13/26:

1) Index Industries

Real estate infrastructure company @Index_inds  raised $50M in a Seed round led by Lightspeed Venture Partners, with participation from Polychain Capital, Galaxy Ventures, Wintermute Ventures, and others

The company is building a daily U.S. home-price index (USHP) and tokenization infrastructure for housing-linked investment products.

They plan to release its USHP product on Ethereum in 2026 and expand to Solana in 2027.

2) Alta

Onchain banking infrastructure company @altaxyz  raised $47.5M in a Series A led by Index Ventures, with participation from GV, Blackbird Ventures, Square Peg, and Capital 49, bringing total funding to $80 million.

Alta’s blockchain is designed to keep balances, transactions, identities, and compliance policies private while verifying that transactions satisfy required rules. Its first product aims to fund markets just in time and move otherwise idle capital into yield-bearing tokenized assets.

Airwallex is building on Alta, with the collaboration designed to connect its payments infrastructure to local fiat networks across 200 countries and 90 currencies.

Also, Alta’s co-founder, Jack Zhang, has hated on blockchain for a long time. Now he’s a convert!

3) DECA Labs

Agent-led software commercialization network @deca_labs reported $12M in total funding from Polychain Capital, Pantera Capital, Accel, dao5, and others.

Its agents identify product opportunities from market signals, test demand with buyers, and allocate development and distribution resources only to concepts that pass predefined thresholds. The network is built for the Base ecosystem.

The release reports a 100,000-plus waitlist, more than 50,000 market signals analyzed, over 80,000 monthly users across its product fleet, and about $1.5 million in gross revenue to date.

4) Slop Cash

Open-source funding rail @SlopCash opened its public $SLOP token auction after early bids committed at least $400,000 from more than 200 bidders.

Funders set prize pools for open-source repositories, and contributors are rewarded for merged pull requests and accepted code reviews rather than submitted work.

Terribly hilarious name but open source needs more funding methods!

5) Marble

Institutional trading and AI-infrastructure finance company @marblegroupxyz raised an $11M Seed round led by Polychain Capital, with participation from Maven 11, Ripple, Susquehanna Crypto, Lattice, and others.

Marble Compute arranges private-credit financing for GPU operators and neoclouds, including compute forwards for future capacity. Marble Markets is building institutional trading across digital assets, real-world assets, prediction markets, and compute.

Co-CEO Matt Ballensweig previously led global trading at BitGo, while co-CEO Leon Marshall was CEO of Galaxy Digital’s European business. Nice team.

text:
There’s a lot unfolding around Nvidia right now.

But beyond the immediate headlines, what interests me most is what Jensen Huang’s departure could mean for the broader AI economy, given the extraordinary scale and reach of Nvidia’s influence.

Most people know Nvidia as the company behind the chips powering the AI boom. But its involvement extends far beyond semiconductors.

Through its technology, strategic investments, partnerships, and increasingly substantial financing arrangements, Nvidia has become deeply embedded across the AI economy, including financing the very ecosystem that drives demand for its own technology.

Jensen Huang has often described the AI economy as a five-layer cake: energy, chips, infrastructure, models, and applications.

What’s remarkable is the extent to which Nvidia has established influence and financial relationships across all five layers.

1. Energy

Nvidia’s influence extends into the electricity infrastructure required to power the AI economy.

In March 2026, Nvidia and Emerald AI announced a collaboration with six major energy companies, including NextEra Energy, Constellation, AES, and Vistra, to develop AI data centers that can interact with electricity grids and accelerate access to power.

Nvidia also committed $3 billion to SB Energy, including $1.5 billion already funded, supporting the development of an 8-gigawatt AI data center campus in Ohio for OpenAI.

2. Chips

Nvidia’s core business extends into a vast semiconductor supply chain involving TSMC, advanced memory suppliers, and manufacturing partners.

The company has committed hundreds of billions of dollars to securing the production capacity and components required for future generations of AI systems.

3. Infrastructure

Nvidia’s involvement goes well beyond supplying the computing systems installed in AI data centers.

It invested another $2 billion in CoreWeave, supporting plans to develop more than 5 gigawatts of AI data center capacity by 2030.

It’s also providing up to $105 billion in financial guarantees for an Ohio data center project developed by SB Energy for OpenAI.

And Nvidia has agreements to purchase computing capacity from cloud providers deploying its own infrastructure, helping support demand for the facilities those companies are building.

But its financing ambitions extend much further.

In August 2026, Nvidia announced partnerships with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs, and KKR to mobilize more than $500 billion in outside investment to finance AI infrastructure.

Huang also outlined plans for Nvidia to potentially provide financial backing for up to 25% of that financing, helping attract institutional capital to infrastructure built around its own technology.

4. Models

Nvidia has established strategic investment relationships with leading AI model developers, including Anthropic, while supplying the computing infrastructure supporting their development.

It’s also developing its own AI model families, including Nemotron, Cosmos, and GR00T, expanding its influence beyond the hardware used to train and run AI.

5. Applications

Nvidia is extending its reach into robotics, autonomous vehicles, healthcare, and enterprise AI.

One example is its partnership with Eli Lilly, involving plans to jointly invest up to $1 billion over five years in AI-powered drug discovery.

And the financial commitments behind this ecosystem are substantial.

In its latest quarterly filing, Nvidia disclosed:

→ $99 billion in existing equity investments
→ $25 billion committed to additional equity investments
→ $279 billion in supply and capacity commitments
→ $36 billion in AI cloud agreements
→ $108.5 billion in maximum gross financial guarantee exposure, including the SB Energy agreement

Nvidia has been building an interconnected ecosystem in which it supplies the technology, invests in companies developing AI, helps finance the infrastructure they need, and supports the expansion of demand for its own products.

That gives Nvidia extraordinary influence across the entire AI economy, while creating increasingly significant financial and commercial dependencies between the company and its partners.

And that’s what makes Jensen Huang’s departure so consequential. The implications extend far beyond Nvidia itself.

Jensen Huang's resignation — what it means for NVDA and the AI industry
The resignation — verified:
Thursday, November 12, around 8:48 AM ET, Nvidia announced Jensen Huang resigned as President, CEO and board member, effective immediately, ending a 33-year tenure. He co-founded the company in 1993.
Interim CEO: CFO Colette Kress (EVP + CFO since September 2013, keeping the CFO role); the permanent search is internal and external. Harvey C. Jones was appointed the company's first-ever Chair of the Board.
The 8-K: the board accepted the resignation on November 11, effective immediately; the company gave no reason. "Firing" is Rep. Moolenaar's word, not the fact — his own statement's title says "Resignation."
Market reaction: Wednesday's close of $173.73 → pre-market $157.54 (-9.32%, about $400 billion of market value erased) → Thursday's close $165.77 → Friday $162.85 (-2.01%). NVDA fell 12.75% on the week.
Analysts: Ives $225 (without Huang) vs $300 (with him); Stifel $315 → $205; BofA $350 → $280; William Blair cut to Market Perform.
Rotation: AMD +18.93% on the week (Friday -8.75% to $534.06), AVGO up about 19% on the week (Friday $347.01, -4.76%). The NVDA–AMD spread is about -$371. Red pen: AMD trades at 38.44x forward earnings vs NVDA at 13.72x; the scale gap is about 11–13x (NVDA's data-center quarter is about $75 billion, AMD's $6.7 billion).
Three structural breaks for the AI industry:
The founder premium is gone: "Jensen is Nvidia" no longer holds, and the market has to re-price succession uncertainty.
A succession vacuum: Kress is an interim CEO from finance, with no product or visionary pull. In your framework: "NVDA doesn't need an operator, it needs a visionary."
The scrutiny continues: the Senate and House will investigate the Trump administration's approval of Nvidia chip exports to China; Huang has agreed to testify before Congress on the Alice Huang matter before Thanksgiving (no date set). The Warren + Coons preservation letter requires confirmation by November 17.
Rumors and investigations (reported, not established):
The NYT reported an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, his direct report; Reuters reported an intimate relationship with a second employee (two sources, unnamed). Both are allegations, not findings.
The Alice Huang spy case: CNN reported that intelligence to date "does not prove" she spied for Beijing (not an exoneration); the FBI probe is ongoing, with no official finding. CNBC reported she owned stakes in Chinese businesses that provided computing power to Huawei (source reporting, not a finding).
Your rule has fired: the November 11 rule — liquidate NVDA holdings once the CEO is replaced — has fired. The $200 calendar spread (long Jun 17, 2027 $200 calls / short Dec 24, 2026 $200 calls, $12.18 debit) is confirmed held, with a maximum loss of $1,218 per spread. The next test: NVDA earnings Tuesday after the close, Kress's first print facing analysts — watch data-center demand, H200 sales to China, and guidance.
Earnings breakdown: CoreWeave (CRWV) — beat-and-raise, sold on leverage
Q3 (Nov 10, after the close): revenue $3.661 billion, +168% YoY, beating consensus of about $3.5 billion and the company's $3.4–$3.6 billion guide; GAAP EPS -$1.27, beating Zacks' -$1.45 (Finnhub shows -$0.95, a different basis); net loss $709 million.
Profits: adjusted operating income $379 million, beating the $200–$260 million guide; GAAP operating income $207 million. The Sankey: revenue $3.7B → gross profit $2.5B (68%) → operating profit $0.2B (6%) → interest $0.8B + tax and other $0.1B → net loss $0.7B.
Red pen: Q3 net interest expense of $846 million is more than 4x operating profit; Q4 interest is guided at $1.05–$1.15 billion; debt is $46.9 billion. R&D of $2.0 billion is 55% of revenue. 98% of revenue comes from committed contracts ($3.6B) — revenue quality is high; the problem is cost and leverage.
Guidance: backlog $132.5 billion (+138% YoY); FY26 revenue guided up to $13.0–$13.3 billion; capex $37–$39 billion; active power over 1.7 GW; operating cash flow $1.975 billion; cash $6.5 billion.
The stock: Nov 11 close $60.77 → Nov 12 $56.60 → Friday intraday $52.27 (-7.66%, low $49.24). A beat-and-raise sold off — that's the leverage story, not the revenue story.
The slide's numbers were checked against the official print; US $3.4B + rest of world $0.2B sums to $3.6B vs the $3.7B total — a $0.1B rounding difference.
Earnings breakdown: Nebius (NBIS) — a big beat, and the stock fell
Q3 (Nov 12, before the open): adjusted EPS $0.31, revenue $980.8 million; revenue +571% YoY (Q3 2025: $146.1 million) and +68% QoQ (Q2 2026: $582.3 million). Adjusted EBITDA $465.8 million.
Slide check: EPS consensus -$0.63 vs actual $0.31 (a 149% beat); revenue consensus $907.17 million vs actual $980.8 million (an 8% beat). The revenue consensus varies by vendor — the slide's $907.17 million matches MarketBeat, Finnhub's $925.68 million is the high outlier; the beat is large either way.
Red pen one: the slide's "EPS +178% YoY / +358% QoQ" uses the absolute-negative-base convention — the reality is a swing from loss to profit (YoY -$0.40 → +$0.31; QoQ -$0.12 → +$0.31). Don't say +178%.
Red pen two: FY26 revenue guidance was cut to the low end of the $3.0–$3.4 billion range (FactSet $3.35 billion); 2026 capex was raised to about $27 billion (from $20–$25 billion); 2027 capex is $40–$45 billion, far above the expected $28.77 billion; $7 billion-plus ARR was pushed from December to February; about $325 million of Q3 revenue was non-recurring.
Prepayments are the bright spot: Q3 new deals had prepayments covering over 100% of related capex (Q2: 50–60%); over 90% of Q3 contract value carries a prepayment (up about 20 points); deferred revenue on the balance sheet is $9.4 billion (from $1.6 billion at end-2025); payback on 1–3 year deals is 19 months (Q2: 22 months); 2027 prepayments are expected at $17–$20 billion (2026: $10 billion). Customers are paying to fund the build-out.
The stock: Nov 11 close $154.69 → Nov 12 $128.64 (-16.84%) → Friday intraday about $117 (-8.92%, low $109), about -24% in two days; one month -37.01%; 52-week high $299.86.
NBIS continued: 2027 revenue guidance is about 4x — but the market is pricing capex
Revenue trajectory: 2024 $92 million → 2025 $530 million → 2026 guide about $3.0 billion (low end of the range; analysts expect $3.37 billion) → 2027 guide $12–$13 billion, about 4x 2026 (analysts expect $11.98 billion). Q3 was $981 million, +571% YoY, beating the expected $908 million.
Quarterly outlook (VJN estimates): Q3 2026 about $0.9B, Q4 about $1.5B; 2027 Q1 about $2.2B, Q2 about $2.7B, Q3 about $3.2B, Q4 about $4.0B; 2028 Q1 about $4.6B, Q2 $5.2B. Everything after Q3 2026 is an estimate (e), not actuals.
Why a big beat still fell: revenue and EPS both beat big, but guidance was cut, capex jumped, ARR was delayed, and $325 million of revenue was non-recurring — the market is pricing the speed of the cash burn, not the speed of revenue. Prepayments covering 100%+ of capex are a guardrail, not a guarantee.
Against CRWV: both are "revenue exploding, interest and capex exploding faster" AI infrastructure stories; CRWV's interest is 4x its operating profit, and NBIS's capex guide is about 50% above expectations. This week the market chose to sell first and ask later.
Anthropic IPO — the price range is out; the seven giants are putting in $26 billion
Price range: $70–$78 (S-1/A No. 2, Nov 10); about 825 million shares offered, raising $57.75–$64.35 billion; on shares outstanding the valuation is about $916 billion–$1.02 trillion, midpoint about $968 billion — about equal to the May Series H mark of $965 billion.
Fully diluted: at $78, up to about $1.404 trillion (TechCrunch) — a different yardstick from the $1.02 trillion on shares outstanding; both numbers are real.
The $26B concurrent placement (Class N non-voting shares, at the IPO price): Alphabet $10 billion, NVIDIA $10 billion, AMD $2.5 billion, Broadcom $1 billion, Micron $1 billion, Microsoft $1 billion, TSMC $0.5 billion — exactly $26.0 billion in total. All seven buyers are also Anthropic's chip and cloud suppliers.
Timing: pricing reportedly Nov 18, first trade Nov 19 — unconfirmed; the filing carries no date. The founders keep 50.1% voting control through a single Class F share; the lock-up releases in stages (some non-founder insiders can sell 10% on day one).
Anthropic results: Q3 revenue $16.96 billion, compute ate 58%
Q3 2026: revenue $16.956 billion, +1,127% YoY, +47% QoQ (Q2 was +144% — growth is slowing); compute and infrastructure cost $9.863 billion, 58% of revenue; GAAP operating loss $567 million; adjusted operating income $2.463 billion, a 15% margin.
The Sankey: revenue $17.0B — consumption-based $13.2B (78%, API and app token usage), subscription $3.7B (22%, Claude fixed-fee plans); customers over $100K: 11,900+ (+1,153% YoY), net revenue retention 900%. Operating expenses $17.5B: compute $9.9B (58%), personnel $1.7B (10%), sales and marketing $2.4B (14%), other $3.6B (21%); operating loss $0.6B (-3% margin).
GAAP net loss of $23.29 billion is mostly a $21.9 billion non-cash note revaluation — not cash burned. Nine-month revenue is $33.24 billion, net loss $104.04 billion. Long-term commitments are about $900.9 billion (about $70.7 billion due within a year); the annualized run-rate at Oct 31 is about $81 billion; net proceeds are $84.6–$93.7 billion (including the placement).
Your position: you hold pre-IPO Anthropic shares (via Forge Global) and will not chase the IPO. On Nov 9, Claude Fable 5.2 + Mythos 5.2 launched ($8/$40 per million tokens, 20% cheaper than 5.1).
Against OpenAI: the same quarter, OpenAI had revenue of $10 billion and an adjusted operating loss of $10.9 billion (the loss exceeded revenue); Anthropic had revenue of $17 billion and an operating loss of $567 million. Both are burning money — Anthropic's unit economics are closer to breakeven.
Next week: NVDA and WMT earnings; the FOMC minutes are the key
NVDA earnings (Tuesday after the close):
Kress's first earnings as interim CEO, facing analysts. Watch three things: data-center demand, H200 sales to China, and guidance. The first print since the resignation — the market wants to know whether "NVDA without Jensen can still deliver." November 17 is also the date in the Warren + Coons preservation letter; the congressional probe is heating up.
WMT earnings (Thursday before the open):
Q3 FY27, released 6:00 AM CT Thursday, call at 7:00 AM CT (CEO John Furner + CFO John David Rainey). Consensus EPS $0.64 (Zacks, +3.2% YoY), revenue about $186.52 billion (Zacks) / $187.27 billion (TipRanks). Options imply about ±7%; last time (Aug 20) the stock moved just +0.10% the next day.
Watch: high-income customers, e-commerce, and the holiday-season outlook. WMT rose 1.51% on Friday — one of the few green defensive names.
Next-week macro calendar:
Mon 11/16: Empire State manufacturing (Nov); Fed Chair Warsh speaks at 12:00 PM; Williams speaks. POWL earnings after the close; SGRX begins trading split-adjusted (1-for-8).
Tue 11/17: retail sales (Oct) 8:30 AM, +0.2% expected; industrial production 9:15 AM; NAHB housing index. NVDA earnings after the close; HD and DIS before the open.
Wed 11/18: housing starts and building permits (Oct) 8:30 AM; FOMC minutes 2:00 PM. Anthropic pricing reportedly due; TGT, TJX and LOW before the open; PANW after the close.
Thu 11/19: initial jobless claims 8:30 AM; Philly Fed manufacturing; new home sales. WMT earnings before the open; PDD and BABA before the open; Anthropic first trade reportedly due.
Fri 11/20: Michigan consumer sentiment (Nov, final) 10:00 AM. SPCX Nov 20 $144 calls expire; FOMC meets Dec 8–9.
Note: the earnings-calendar graphic has two small errors (Monday after the close, "MONTAUK" is labeled BEKE; Wednesday before the open, ICCM appears twice) — neither affects the NVDA / WMT dates.
This week's key economic data
Two stories this week: inflation isn't cooling fast enough, and housing gave way first. Labor is still tight; long-end demand is weak.
Tue 11/10: CPI MoM (Oct) +0.4% actual vs +0.3% expected (prior +0.6%)
Tue 11/10: Core CPI MoM (Oct) +0.3% actual vs +0.2% expected (prior +0.3%)
Thu 11/12: Initial jobless claims (week ended 11/7) 200,000 vs ~195,000 expected (prior 189,000)
Thu 11/12: 30-year Treasury auction ($25B) tailed 0.4bp
Thu 11/12: Existing-home sales (Oct, SAAR) 3.75 million vs 3.85 million expected (prior 3.97 million)
Thu 11/12: UK GDP QoQ (Q3, first estimate) +0.7% vs +0.7% expected (prior +0.5%)
Fri 11/13: PPI MoM (Oct) +0.3% actual vs +0.4% expected (prior revised up to +1.4%)
CPI (Tuesday, hotter than expected): core is +0.3% for a third straight month, about 3.7% annualized — far above the 2% target; shelter +0.3%, food +0.5%, energy +0.7%. Market reaction: gold fell about 2.5%, the 10-year jumped 12–13bp to about 4.99%, briefly touching 5.01%. Waller: a +0.3% core would make him consider a 50bp hike in December.
CPI year-over-year red pen: the BLS published no 12-month change for October — October 2025 prices were never collected because of the government shutdown, so there is nothing to compare against. The 3.7% / 2.6% on the calendar graphic are September's official numbers, not October's. The Cleveland Fed nowcasts October YoY at about 3.8% headline / 2.6% core; an independent BLS-method estimate is about 4.0% / 2.8%. Year-over-year returns with November CPI (published Dec 10).
PPI (Friday, cooler on the surface): MoM +0.3%, below the +0.4% consensus — but September was revised up to +1.4% (from +1.3%), so the base is hotter; YoY +6.5%, the biggest since November 2022. After PPI, December hike pricing is about 88% for +25bp / 12% for +50bp; the long end did not rally on the PPI.
Labor and the auction (Thursday): initial claims of 200,000 beat the ~195,000 consensus but are still below the 200,000 line (as they have been since mid-September); the prior 189,000 was the lowest since 1969. The $25B 30-year auction tailed 0.4bp (high yield 5.441%), with dealers taking 11.4% (highest since June) — weak long-end demand is part of the bear steepening.
Housing (Thursday, a 16-year low): existing-home sales of 3.75 million SAAR, -5.5% MoM and -8.8% YoY, the lowest since August 2010 and below the 3.85 million consensus. Inventory is 1.59 million homes (5.1 months of supply); the median price is $416,700 (+0.4% YoY). NAR chief economist Yun: mortgage rates are the highest since 2000 (except one month in 2023); the October 30-year mortgage averaged 7.33% (September: 6.86%). October pending home sales (out Nov 18) are the next check; HD and LOW report next week.
UK GDP (Thursday, as expected): Q3 first estimate +0.7% QoQ, matching the Bank of England's November forecast and above Q2's +0.5%; YoY +1.9%. Services +0.9% led, production +0.1%, construction -0.7%. September MoM +0.2%, August revised to 0.0%. First estimates get revised (mean absolute revision 0.27pp); the next estimate is Dec 22. Little direct impact on US stocks; the global growth backdrop is mildly positive.
The week's verdict: inflation is not out of control, but it is not cooling enough to breathe easy either — core is +0.3% for a third straight month and a December hike is fully priced; the long end is steepening on term premium plus weak auction demand, not on growth panic; labor is still tight while housing is the first to break under high rates. Next week's data tests: Tuesday retail sales, Wednesday's FOMC minutes.
Sources: the user's economic calendar graphic (Trading Economics basis); CPI / PPI from the BLS, existing-home sales from NAR, UK GDP from the ONS, initial claims and the 30-year auction from verified US Treasury / Labor Department figures. The CPI YoY column was corrected after cross-checking — see the red pen above.
This week's personal trade log — 13 trades, all long calls
NVDA calendar spread, 100 spreads: long Jun 17, 2027 $200 calls / short Dec 24, 2026 $200 calls — $12.18 debit. Short leg expires Dec 24 (41 days). Friday close $162.85. Target $200 (+22.8%). Confirmed held; max loss $1,218 per spread.
AVGO Jan 21, 2028 $370 calls — $52.12. Expiry Jan 21, 2028 (434 days). Friday close $347.01. Breakeven $422.12 (+21.6%). 6.6% out of the money; 52-week high $495.
MRNA Jun 17, 2027 $370 calls — $47.70. Expiry Jun 17, 2027 (216 days). Friday close $223.37. Breakeven $417.70 (+87.0%). 65.6% out of the money; the card's breakeven was $399.50 — differs from the log.
POWL Dec 17, 2027 $180 calls — $31.50. Expiry Dec 17, 2027 (399 days). Friday close $142.72. Breakeven $211.50 (+48.2%). 26.1% out of the money; earnings Monday after the close.
INTC Dec 11, 2026 $75 calls — $0.71. Expiry Dec 11, 2026 (28 days). Friday close $59.66. Breakeven $75.71 (+26.9%). 25.7% out of the money; +27% in 28 days — a lottery ticket.
SKHY Feb 19, 2027 $140 calls — $15.00. Expiry Feb 19, 2027 (98 days). Friday close $131.79. Breakeven $155.00 (+17.6%). 6.2% out of the money; spans the Jan 28 earnings.
MRNA Dec 18, 2026 $320 calls — $6.70. Expiry Dec 18, 2026 (35 days). Friday close $223.37. Breakeven $326.70 (+46.3%). 43.3% out of the money; +46% in 35 days — a lottery ticket.
INO Jan 15, 2027 $1.50 calls — premium not provided. Expiry Jan 15, 2027 (63 days). Friday close $1.43. No breakeven (cost not provided). 4.9% out of the money; the closest to the money on the whole sheet.
INTC Mar 19, 2027 $80 calls — $4.10. Expiry Mar 19, 2027 (126 days). Friday close $59.66. Breakeven $84.10 (+41.0%). 34.1% out of the money; spans the January earnings; matches the card's $4.09.
TSLA Jan 15, 2027 $500 calls — $4.20. Expiry Jan 15, 2027 (63 days). Friday close $390.22. Breakeven $504.20 (+29.2%). 28.1% out of the money; expires before the Q4 print — not an earnings ticket.
AMD Feb 19, 2027 $700 calls — $20.70. Expiry Feb 19, 2027 (98 days). Friday close $534.06. Breakeven $720.70 (+34.9%). 31.1% out of the money; breakeven above the 52-week high of $658.52.
AMD Feb 19, 2027 $870 calls — $6.05. Expiry Feb 19, 2027 (98 days). Friday close $534.06. Breakeven $876.05 (+64.0%). 62.9% out of the money; your $6.05 is below the card's $7.00; the most extreme leg on the book.
TSLA Dec 15, 2028 $900 calls — $23.35. Expiry Dec 15, 2028 (763 days). Friday close $390.22. Breakeven $923.35 (+136.6%). 130.6% out of the money; a LEAP spanning about 8 earnings cycles; the card printed $22.80.
Overall read:
All long options: 13 trades, and except for the NVDA calendar spread, all are long calls — no puts, no short sales. One direction, one kind of leverage.
Concentrated in AI / semis: AVGO, INTC x2, SKHY, AMD x2, NVDA and POWL (data-center power equipment) are 9 of the 13; MRNA x2, INO and TSLA x2 are the satellites.
Three time layers: near-month lottery tickets (Dec 11 INTC $75 and Dec 18 MRNA $320, needing +27% / +46% to break even); February earnings tickets (SKHY $140, AMD $700, AMD $870, spanning Q4 earnings); long-dated thesis tickets (AVGO $370, POWL $180, TSLA $900 LEAP).
Card vs log differences: the MRNA $370 call card implies a premium of about $29.50 (breakeven $399.50) vs your logged $47.70 (breakeven $417.70) — go with your cost. AMD $870 calls: your $6.05 is below the card's $7.00; TSLA $900 calls: your $23.35 is above the card's $22.80; SKHY $15.00 is below the card's implied $17.20; POWL $31.50 is slightly above the card's implied $30.09.
The NVDA calendar spread: your November 11 rule (liquidate NVDA once the CEO is replaced) has fired, and this spread falls inside it. The short $200 leg is 22.8% out of the money with 41 days left — time is on the short leg's side; the long leg has 216 days and wants NVDA to repair toward $200.
Friday closes: Finnhub (Nov 13, 2026 close, cross-checked across sources). Premiums and strikes are quoted verbatim from your fill records; INO's cost was not provided, so there is no breakeven for it.
Next-week battle checklist
Sat 11/14, about 1:17 PM: Starship Ship catch attempt — the biggest remaining catalyst for the SPCX Nov 20 $144 calls (breakeven $150.00); the booster already missed, so a full double catch is off the table.
Mon 11/16: POWL earnings after the close (your Dec 17, 2027 $180 calls are held); SGRX begins trading split-adjusted (1-for-8); Empire State manufacturing; Warsh speaks.
Tue 11/17 after the close: NVDA earnings — the week's biggest event. Retail sales at 8:30 AM before the open (+0.2% expected). SPX key levels: up through 7,622.50, down through 7,500.12.
Wed 11/18, 2:00 PM: FOMC minutes — the most yield-moving item of the week. Anthropic pricing reportedly due. 10-year: watch R1 51.80 / S1 51.21.
Thu 11/19 before the open: WMT earnings (consensus EPS $0.64, revenue about $186.5B). Anthropic first trade reportedly due. Initial claims at 8:30 AM.
Fri 11/20: Michigan sentiment (final) at 10:00 AM; SPCX Nov 20 $144 calls expire; FOMC meets Dec 8–9.
Semis: SMH — up through R1 500.26, down through S1 473.25; SOXX — up through R1 154.23, down through S1 144.50; the 200-day (SMH 523.77 / SOXX 160.27) is the real resistance.
Volatility: VIX — up through R1 20.93, down through S1 17.65; MOVE — up through R1 100.89, down through S1 97.56. "True fear" needs VIX above 20 AND MOVE above 100 at the same time.
Rates: the 2-year reclaiming 4.868 or breaking 4.826 is the directional signal; the 5-year is about the 5.00% line; the long end is pressed against the upper Bollinger band — don't chase.
Position discipline: all 13 trades are long calls — one direction. The two near-month lottery tickets (Dec 11 INTC $75, Dec 18 MRNA $320) have only 28 / 35 days left; the thing to manage is time, not direction.
One line: the broad market sits on its pivot, semis sit below theirs, rates sit on the upper band, volatility sits at the door of 20 — next week's answer comes Tuesday after the close from NVDA, not from Monday's open.
Appendix: this week's earnings calendar (week of Nov 9)

NBIS (Thu before the open): revenue $980.8M (+571% YoY), EPS $0.31, a swing from loss to profit — but guidance was cut and capex jumped, and the stock fell about 24% in two days.

Friday before the open: PAVM, SBC, RMX, MIST, NDLS, EOC, EIC, BRAG, BSP, WRD.

Michigan has scored just 12 points in its last two games. Now the Wolverines face an Oregon team averaging 73.7 offensive snaps per game.

Can Michigan’s elite defense keep this close without help from its offense?

📊 FAIR MARKET
• Fair Spread: Oregon -13.5 | Market: -10.5
• Fair Total: 37.5 | Market: 38.5
• Fair ML: Oregon -426 / Michigan +426
• Confidence: 62/100

🎯 SCORE PREDICTION
🟢 Oregon 26
🟡 Michigan 12

🧠 HOW THIS GAME PLAYS OUT
• Passing mismatch: Oregon owns a 71.9 PFF passing grade versus Michigan’s 63.5. Under pressure, Oregon’s passer rating advantage is 73.0 to 40.1.
• Defensive resistance: Michigan ranks 20th defensively by PFF’s power rankings. Oregon ranks third. Both defenses should create difficult early-down situations.
• Offensive consistency: Michigan averages just 64.6 snaps and posts -0.16 EPA per rush. Oregon runs 73.7 plays with positive EPA rushing and passing.
• Game script: Expect a competitive first half before Oregon’s offensive volume and Michigan’s inability to sustain drives create separation.

🔑 X-Factor: Michigan’s offensive line against Oregon’s front seven. If the Wolverines cannot establish the run, their passing efficiency may not survive obvious passing situations.

⚠️ MARKET CHECK
Our fair spread favors Oregon by three additional points. Several odds trackers show movement from Oregon -13.5 to -10.5, although opening prices vary by sportsbook.
That three-point move against our projection triggers the MIDP adverse-movement guardrail. The football projection stays unchanged, but the betting classification is PASS pending stronger confirmation.
